title: FlexGaze: Weakly Supervised Gaze Estimation at Scale
abstract: Most gaze estimation models are trained on data collected using specialized equipment. The limited diversity of subjects, scenes, and head poses in these datasets hinders generalization to new conditions. We present FlexGaze, a family of 3D gaze estimators pretrained with weak supervision from gaze labels (pseudo-labels) automatically generated from in-the-wild images. We use off-the-shelf models to predict 2D gaze targets and scene depth, then combine these predictions to generate 3D gaze labels for approximately 3.24 million head instances. At inference, FlexGaze predicts gaze from a head crop alone and can handle profile and rear views without requiring face detection or head pose estimation. We use data augmentation during training to improve robustness to variations in crop position and scale. Pretrained using only these generated gaze labels, FlexGaze generalizes to unseen benchmarks. After supervised fine-tuning on public gaze datasets, we evaluate FlexGaze on eight benchmarks under a unified evaluation protocol. Our models match or outperform publicly available gaze estimators with several times as many parameters on most benchmarks. We release our dataset of generated gaze labels, all trained models, and code via https://github.com/ihp-lab/FlexGaze.

title: EEG Decoding in Context: A Framework for Tuning-Free EEG Foundation Models
abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) decoding is a central route toward brain-computer interfaces for communication, rehabilitation, cognitive assessment, and neurological monitoring. Recent EEG foundation models have substantially advanced reusable signal representations, but their downstream use still typically requires a task-specific decoder, gradient-based adaptation, and validation-driven model selection. We investigate a complementary foundation-model paradigm based on in-context learning: labeled EEG recordings define the decoding task as context, and new recordings are predicted without updating model parameters. We first pair raw EEG features with a pretrained general-purpose in-context predictor. This direct formulation provides a promising starting point, but its performance remains limited and unstable and does not generalize reliably across EEG paradigms. We find that suitable context construction can address these limitations by improving the effective signal-to-noise ratio and exposing temporal and spatial structure. Building on this insight, we introduce a general framework that combines EEG-specific context construction with a frozen in-context predictor and a metric-based context adaptation mechanism, which matches each downstream task to an appropriate context representation without relying on validation data. Across ten datasets spanning seven EEG decoding paradigms, our method achieves the highest mean BAcc among eleven specialized and fine-tuned EEG baselines, without task-specific parameter updates or validation-based model selection. This framework provides a practical path toward tuning-free EEG foundation models in which adaptation is expressed through context rather than parameter updates.

title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
abstract: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.

title: Precision-Aware Learning Rate Transfer Across Block Count in LLM Post-Training
abstract: The post-training of pretrained large language models, including supervised finetuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), is very sensitive to the learning rate, and tuning it through grid search is costly in both computation and memory. In this work, we propose \textbf{TipSweep}, a method to transfer the learning rate across the number of trainable transformer blocks. To do so efficiently, we search for the best learning rate by training only the last $k_0$ blocks (in our experiments, typically $k_0=1$), and provide scaling rules that predict the optimal learning rate when training any set of $k$ blocks, including when $k=L$ (the full transformer). Across experiments with models ranging from 1 to 7 billion parameters, we observe that the optimal learning rate follows precision-dependent scaling rules: the optimal rate scales approximately as $k^{-1}$ with float32 (FP32) master weights, but as $k^{-1/2}$ when updates are applied directly to bfloat16 (BF16) weights without a master copy. We explain both rules using an analytical model that accounts for update rounding, under assumptions supported by profiling experiments. Finally, we develop two prototypes of the learning rate search for a 6.7-billion-parameter model. The first fits the search on a single consumer GPU with 16 GiB of memory. The second speeds up the search on a high-end GPU by evaluating all candidate learning rates in a single pass over the data, so that a five-candidate search takes about half the GPU hours of one full-depth ($k=L$) run.

title: Aligning Judge Models to Be Logically Consistent Multi-Rule Interpreters
abstract: Technical governance of AI models will soon require them to reason over and follow thousands of rules from different jurisdictions. However, as we show in this work, presenting an entire ruleset to a judge model---rather than asking it to judge one rule at a time---changes the way the model interprets the requirements, making it reach conclusions that conflict with its rule-by-rule judgments. We call this challenge multi-rule inconsistency and find that models are more lenient when judging rules embedded within the full ruleset than when judging rules separately. For example, we find that when a safety-critical rule prohibiting a model from pursuing objectives other than those it was given appears in a larger ruleset, all tested judge models are less likely to deem it violated. We examine several methods for reducing inconsistency, including prompting, consistency training using GRPO, and iterative rule refinement. As in human statutory interpretation, surrounding rules shape how a rule is interpreted. Unlike the legal setting, however, these interactions are currently happening implicitly inside the judge model's reasoning. We argue that multi-rule interactions must be measured and handled explicitly by ruleset designers to prevent undetected shifts in interpretation from causing downstream alignment failures.

title: When Does Overriding the Majority Vote Help?
abstract: When should additional reasoning or verification replace a majority-vote answer? We call such a replacement an override. We examine two obstacles: the availability of correct alternatives and the reliability of methods that produce or select them. We compare additional reasoning, executed programs, and cross-model reasoning on 150 competition-mathematics questions with three open reasoning models. Starting from a majority vote over 16 responses, we measure how often overrides occur and how many errors they correct or introduce across agreement thresholds. When the vote is incorrect, the correct answer is often absent from the original responses. Additional same-model reasoning rarely overrides, while executed programs correct more errors than they introduce at every evaluated threshold. Cross-model overrides improve some weaker baselines but do not establish an advantage over the more accurate model alone, even with only eight standalone responses. Stricter agreement reduces how often overrides occur but does not consistently increase the fraction that correct errors. At the strictest thresholds, overrides occur on few distinct questions, limiting conclusions about their reliability.

title: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control
abstract: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138times while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

title: ArchTopic - LLM-Enhanced Framework for Archival Topic Extraction and Thematic Clustering
abstract: Concise topic tagging of individual records enhances searchability and supports targeted thematic analysis within large archival corpora. Aggregating these tags into higher-level representations enables macro-scale pattern discovery and user-centric navigation across heterogeneous historical datasets. To meet these objectives, we developed a three-stage computational framework named ArchTopic - LLM-Enhanced Framework for Archival Topic Extraction and Thematic Clustering. Stage 1 applies zero-shot prompting with the LLaMA 3.2 3B model for context-driven topic extraction. Stage 2 enforces semantic alignment between generated topics and source texts through multilingual embedding comparison, cosine-similarity thresholding, and iterative refinement via a dual-LLM ensemble. Stage 3 builds a higher-level representation of the entire corpus by concatenating validated text and topic embeddings, reducing dimensionality with UMAP for topology preservation, clustering with k-means determined by the elbow criterion, and labeling clusters using YAKE (Yet Another Keyword Extractor) augmented with LLM-guided label synthesis. Our evaluation of more than 180,000 administrative correspondence records (1581–1859) from the Portuguese Overseas Historical Archive (Arquivo Histórico Ultramarino), specifically the Collection of Conselho Ultramarino, shows that the proposed framework produces well-separated, semantically coherent clusters, while embedding-space visualizations and word-cloud analyses confirm thematic integrity. We validate the framework’s superior cluster distinctiveness, label coherence, and computational throughput through comparative benchmarks against traditional Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and BERTopic approaches. Integrated LLM prompting, embedding validation, and clustering algorithms together establish a reproducible, scalable framework for thematic exploration and intuitive navigation of extensive archival collections. Code: ArchTopic-LLM: An LLM-Enhanced Framework for Archival Topic Extraction and Thematic Clustering (in preparation). Dataset: MAPE (Mapping the Atlantic Portuguese Empire): A historical dataset derived from the Conselho Ultramarino collection of the Portuguese Overseas Historical Archive (Arquivo Histórico Ultramarino), used for topic modelling and thematic analysis of the Portuguese Atlantic Empire. Figures: Visualisations of topic modelling results and thematic clusters identified within the Conselho Ultramarino collection of the Portuguese Overseas Historical Archive (Arquivo Histórico Ultramarino), illustrating the thematic structure and patterns emerging from the archival records. title: SPROUT: Predicting Objective-Grounded Prompt Utility for Efficient Text-to-Image Preference Tuning
abstract: Preference tuning of text-to-image diffusion models spends most of its compute generating candidate images, yet training prompts are typically sampled uniformly at random, wasting compute generating images that provide too little signal for model alignment. To best utilize the available compute, we study prompt selection, where at each iteration we identify the most useful prompts for preference tuning. We separate prompt selection into a utility score, an estimator of that utility score, and batch selection. Within this framework, we propose Selection by PRedicting Objective-grounded UTility (SPROUT). The utility score is predicted on every prompt in the pool, including unseen prompts, by a text-only model, refit after every iteration on all utilities observed so far. A randomized acceptance rule then turns these predictions into a batch, so no images are generated beyond those used for training. For direct group preference optimization (DGPO), the objective-grounded utility is the norm of the gradient that the objective produces from a prompt's group of images. Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion 1.5 with DGPO on GenEval, SPROUT matches the final score of uniform sampling in about 44% of the iterations and improves the area under the learning curve with respect to both uniform sampling and CGPO, a recent variance-based prompt sampler. The efficiency gains hold under four held-out reward models never used in training, and the ranking of methods carries over to DPG-Bench and T2I-CompBench++. Our code is available at https://github.com/ADDAPT-ML/SPROUT.

title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
abstract: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.

title: Analyzing and Improving FlowMap Distillation of Autoregressive Video Models
abstract: FlowMap distillation offers a natural route to few-step generative modeling by directly learning a teacher's denoising trajectories. Yet for autoregressive (AR) video generation, existing few-step models still rely on distribution matching distillation (DMD) to remain competitive, sacrificing sample diversity and requiring a large bidirectional teacher. In this work, we analyze what limits standalone AR FlowMap distillation and introduce two complementary guidance mechanisms to close this gap: (1) anti-drifting guidance, which helps the AR teacher correct drifted student rollouts by training an auxiliary model to mimic student drift and using it as a negative guidance branch; and (2) motion-aware guidance, which makes motion easier for a FlowMap student to learn by locating motion patches and selectively applying skip-layer guidance. title: Ego2Wrist: Bootstrapping Wrist-View Synthesis from Egocentric Video
abstract: Wrist cameras provide an action-centric view that is directly relevant to robot manipulation. However, collecting human wrist-camera videos at scale is challenging due to cumbersome setups that can interfere with natural hand movements. In contrast, head-mounted human egocentric videos are much easier to scale. We introduce Ego2Wrist, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Trained on approximately 940 hours of paired head- and wrist-camera recordings, Ego2Wrist jointly generates three views. To evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view. HCC ranks model checkpoints comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS, and human evaluators prefer HCC-selected generations in 77% of responses. Evaluated on four datasets, Ego2Wrist outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander, reducing LPIPS by 28% and receiving human preference in 76% of responses. More importantly, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement on in-the-wild egocentric videos by selecting generated wrist views for further training. Generation quality progressively improves over three rounds. These results demonstrate a scalable approach to generating real-world wrist-view human manipulation videos for robot policy training.

title: Habitats: A Framework for Open-Ended Evolution of Agent Objectives
abstract: Designing what an agent should optimize can be as difficult as optimizing the agent itself. Existing language-model-based reward-generation methods typically refine objectives for predefined tasks and couple the decision of what to explore with the synthesis of how to implement it, potentially narrowing the resulting behavioral repertoire. We introduce Habitats, a framework for open-ended evolution of executable agent objectives. Habitats maintains a population of reward-policy pairs and evaluates every policy under every population reward, producing a cross-fitness matrix that exposes self-mastery, transfer, and functional diversity. A population-level Planner uses this information to select parent rewards and issue targeted mutation directives, while a separate Mutator translates those directives into validated reward programs. We evaluate Habitats in a discrete Card Sandbox and three continuous-control environments (Cart-Pole, Hopper, and Cheetah) against Independent Generation and Direct Mutation baselines. Across four environments and three random seeds, Habitats achieves the highest macro-averaged final Specialist Quality and Behavioral Diversity, with final diversity reaching 1.8x that of Direct Mutation and 2.5x that of Independent Generation. Finally, across ten downstream objectives unseen during evolution, frozen Habitats policy libraries achieve higher paired win rates than size-matched Direct Mutation and Independent Generation libraries at 10,000 adaptation episodes, while also surpassing task-specific policies trained from scratch for 20,000 episodes. These results suggest that separating population-level planning from reward synthesis enables the discovery of diverse, learnable, and reusable behaviors.

title: Tokens as Locality-Preserving Anchors: Scalable Novel View Synthesis with Target-Adaptive Token Routing
abstract: Transformer-based view synthesis models render each target viewpoint from the source images, without an explicit 3D representation, which lets them reproduce fine detail and view-dependent effects. However, their decoder attends to every source token for every frame, so rendering slows with each source image. Rasterization avoids this by culling primitives that the viewpoint does not see, but source tokens cannot be culled this way, as they have no explicit position or extent. Our key insight is that source tokens are nonetheless spatial anchors: each encodes a local region of the scene, so the decoder's attention for any viewpoint concentrates on a few of them. A lightweight router predicts these tokens from the source tokens and the viewpoint, and the decoder attends only to a fixed budget of top-ranked tokens, so its cost no longer depends on the number of source tokens. We supervise the router with the decoder's attention, using non-maximum suppression to demote redundant tokens. With 24 source images and two views' worth of tokens, our model renders 6.4 times faster than LagerNVS, at a PSNR only 0.68 dB lower. One ranking serves every budget, so the budget can change at render time.

title: Typhoon OCR 2: From Thai Document Transcription to Multilingual, Multi-Task OCR
abstract: Typhoon OCR 1.5 focused on reading Thai documents. However, in real-world workflows, users often need to extract specific information or preserve the structure of an entire page for further processing. Typhoon OCR 2 handles both tasks in a single model, with prompt-driven extraction and structured full-page parsing. Full-page parsing covers Thai, English, and Chinese. We release compact 2B and 0.8B models adapted from open document parsers through supervised fine-tuning on curated Thai and public multilingual data, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task rewards and a rule penalizing unfinished responses. Among evaluated open models, Typhoon OCR 2 2B scores highest on Thai MDPBench (80.7 versus 68.9 for Typhoon OCR 1.5) and on ThaiOCRBench (59.91 versus 40.45), which covers recognition, extraction, and document understanding. The 2B model remains close to its base on English olmOCR-bench (84.7 versus 84.4) and on OmniDocBench, which evaluates English and Chinese together (90.97 versus 91.03). On MDPBench, GRPO reduces the mean share of pages with repetition loops for the 2B model from 3.2% to 0.7%, with a smaller and statistically uncertain score gain for the 0.8B model. We release the model weights, Python package, and evaluation suite.

title: Frontier models need only one text to unmask its human or AI author
abstract: Given a single text and a simple zero-shot prompt (no web access, tools, candidate lists, or writing samples), frontier models can answer "who wrote this?" at three increasingly specific levels: (1) whether an AI or human wrote it, (2) if an AI, which lab, and (3) if a human, often exactly who. The latest models (Claude Fable 5.2, GPT-6.1 Sol, Gemini 4 Carbon) match trained detectors like Pangram while also explaining their predictions in natural language, and Opus 5.5 names the correct lab for 98% of texts generated by models from Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google. Most strikingly, Fable 5.2 correctly names the author of 55% of 15K anonymous ICML 2020 reviews that were never made public, and identifies the username behind 69% of comments from active Redditors (with >500 posts over the last year). Accuracy depends on exposure to an author's writing in pretraining data and on reasoning effort, and simply asking a model how familiar it is with someone predicts whether it can identify their writing. For anyone who has published enough writing online, frontier models present a greater threat to anonymity than commonly assumed, and defenses are limited.

title: Optimal Regret Lower Bounds in Matrix Games
abstract: We study learning in two-player zero-sum games, also known as matrix games, in which two players with $m$ and $n$ actions repeatedly select mixed strategies for $T$ rounds. The learning dynamics based on optimistic Hedge guarantee regrets of $O(\log(mn))$, which improve to $O(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$ if each player knows the number of actions of the opponent, whereas matching regret lower bounds have been known only for specific learning dynamics. We prove that, for every deterministic learning dynamic, there exists a payoff matrix for which the maximum individual regret is $Ω(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$ for a wide range of $m$ and $n$. Together with the upper bound $O(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$, this lower bound shows that the minimax regret of deterministic learning dynamics in matrix games is $Θ(\sqrt{\log m\log n})$ in this regime. For all $m$, $n$, and $T$, we also prove the lower bound $Ω(\min\{T,\log\min\{m,n\}\})$. These lower bounds hold even if each player also observes the strategies and the feedback of the opponent. Our main technical contribution is an adaptive construction of the payoff matrix. While running the algorithms of the two players, we add in each round a rank-one matrix that keeps the feedback of the previous rounds unchanged and increases a lower bound on the sum of the regrets of the two players. As by-products, we obtain lower bounds on the rate at which the average strategies converge to a Nash equilibrium and on the query complexity of matrix-vector products that deterministic algorithms need to compute an approximate Nash equilibrium.

title: Head Anything: Correspondence-Guided Joint Generation of 3D Heads from Few Images
abstract: Large image-to-3D generators recover detailed heads from a single photograph but treat every image as a new object. For several images of one person, they hallucinate unseen regions independently without using information from the other images. We present Head Anything, which generates detailed head meshes from a few images with changing expressions and viewpoints. Instead of training a multi-image prior, we turn a pretrained single-image generator with a native 3D latent space into a joint generator that denoises all images together. Since global attention between images is hard to learn from scarce 3D head data, lightweight correspondence-attention adapters let every 3D token attend only to its corresponding points in the other images. We obtain correspondences by fitting a neural parametric head model to the generator's own single-image outputs, requiring no ground truth at test time. Training on both ground-truth and fitted correspondences makes the adapters robust to fitting errors. Each mesh stays pixel-aligned with its own image and borrows the unseen regions from all others. On head scans, Head Anything lowers the head Chamfer distance of the best image-to-3D generator by 32% and its cross-frame inconsistency by 47%, and its meshes improve face tracking. Code and models will be released.

title: Large Language Models in Crowd Management Systems: A Critical Review of Cognitive Intelligence, Applications, and Challenges — Reproducibility Package
abstract: Reproducibility materials accompanying the critical evidence-map review of large language models in crowd management systems. The archive preserves 317 candidate entries, 275 unique candidates, 79 mapped records (38 core and 41 adjacent/supporting), 19 contextual references, and 177 non-retained records. Relevant full-text sections were inspected for 36 of 38 core studies. Of 54 evaluated or simulation records, 30 report explicit comparators and 14 have numerically extracted outcomes. Independent human screening of a random sample of 55 records gave 47/55 three-category agreement (Cohen’s kappa 0.7642). Version 1.1.0 adds a function-by-design evidence map of the 38 core records and an extraction-based nine-item CCIF reporting checklist for 23 direct component and crowd-related task studies (207 criterion-level indications, with locators and reproducible descriptive summaries). The checklist is not an independently validated quality instrument. Original screening decisions and extraction records remain unchanged. Literature cutoff: 22 November 2026. The archive provides exact queries, evidence and access ledgers, anonymized paired decisions, author-approved reconciliation, codebook, six figures and reproducibility scripts. No personal reviewer details, third-party articles, original datasets, live operational records, model implementations or physical control instructions are redistributed.

title: HoloSplat: Real-Time Token Streaming for Feed-Forward Human Reconstruction
abstract: Live free-viewpoint video streaming of humans enables immersive telepresence and interactive XR applications. However, this requires reconstructing each frame in real time, transmitting the data within strict bandwidth budgets, and decoding it on lightweight client GPUs. Existing approaches, whether relying on per-frame optimization or feed-forward inference, generate massive 3D Gaussian payloads that exceed practical streaming limits, while aggressive compression severely degrades rendering quality. In this work, we present HoloSplat, a real-time streaming framework for human-centric volumetric video. HoloSplat splits a feed-forward reconstructor before its Gaussian head, introducing a multi-rate streaming codec driven by server-side token compression and client-side token restoration. On the server side, we apply opacity-guided token pruning, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and lossless geometry coding for token anchors. On the client side, a feature reconstruction hypernetwork is fused into the Gaussian head to recover compression-induced quality loss. Furthermore, we introduce Neural Session Calibration (NSC), which rapidly fine-tunes the Gaussian head online using incoming camera views during a warm-up phase. This resolves quality degradation from novel camera parameters and varying capture conditions with zero per-frame overhead. In our evaluations, HoloSplat averages 32.2 FPS on four RTX 5090 GPUs at 50 Mbit/s. It decodes each frame into 3D Gaussians in 22.1 ms on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop GPU, transmitting 22.8$\times$ less data than uncompressed float32 Gaussians, while calibrated decoding improves PSNR by 1.050 dB.

title: How Organizational AI Ethics Governance Shapes Employee Creativity: A Conceptual Analysis of Mechanisms and Boundary Conditions
abstract: As AI becomes embedded in organizational decision-making and knowledge production, employees gain new tools for accessing and generating information while also confronting concerns about algorithmic evaluation, data use, and accountability. Drawing on research on AI ethics, algorithmic management, and organizational creativity, this conceptual study defines organizational AI ethics governance as the rules, procedures, and allocation of responsibilities that guide the development, deployment, operation, and retirement of AI systems. We argue that such governance can shape employee creativity through several connected mechanisms. Fair and contestable procedures can strengthen procedural justice, while transparent system boundaries and meaningful human review can support calibrated trust. Tolerance for responsible experimentation, together with discretion over how AI is used, can protect psychological safety and job autonomy. Governance also determines whether human–AI collaboration broadens exploration or channels employees toward standardized outputs. These effects depend on task characteristics, the stakes of AI-assisted decisions, whether AI is used primarily for automation or augmentation, employees' AI literacy, and the consistency between formal rules and managerial conduct. This study suggests that organizations should translate ethical principles into risk-based review, purpose limitation in data use, effective contestability and appeal mechanisms, employee participation, and oversight across the AI system life cycle so that AI can serve as a resource for careful creative work rather than a substitute for judgment.

title: Deneb-Vritra: Descriptions, Edges and Names Examined by Blocking Via Restoring Token Representations and Attention
abstract: Laya is a 421M-parameter encoder that answers a question about a text in one pass: each answer option, written as a name plus a description, gets a marker token, and one score is read from the network at each marker. We first confirm that such models can follow an option's name when it contradicts the description; the question is where in the network this happens. We locate it. On 951 synthetic questions we move each name onto another option's description and count how often the model picks the option with the right name (the name shortcut): 53% for the released checkpoint, 59% for our fine-tune v1, 11% for a fine-tune with name randomisation. On a 320-item sample, blocking attention from each marker to its own name tokens in layers 14 to 17 of 28 cuts v1's shortcut from 67% to 16% (19% on two schemas held out from component selection) while accuracy with the original names stays at 90%; blocking marker edges to the question, other options or text has no effect. No single head matters (largest effect 9 points), and restoring clean marker states undoes the swap from layer 16. Attention mass tracks the window by layer but not by head. Repeated on 5 checkpoints (released, fine-tuned, name-randomised, and a pair trained without two schemas), the knockout finds similar layers; in the name-randomised ones, blocking the description edges instead brings the shortcut back to 56-58%, so the read persists and is outvoted. Marker states decode the name from layer 0; a one-direction probe erasure changed nothing but was weaker than a random edit. Copying layers 0-13 or 14-27 of a name-randomised sibling into a fine-tune recovers 66% and 65% (v1); 21% and 45% (pair A) of its shortcut reduction. 9 of the 12 predictions we could score, written before running, failed. Head sweeps cover 5 of 5 checkpoints; data are synthetic and LLM-labelled; one architecture.

On 951 synthetic questions we move each name onto another option's description and count how often the model picks the option with the right name (the name shortcut): 53% for the released checkpoint, 59% for our fine-tune v1, 11% for a fine-tune with name randomisation. On a 320-item sample, blocking attention from each marker to its own name tokens in layers 14 to 17 of 28 cuts v1's shortcut from 67% to 16% (19% on two schemas held out from component selection) while accuracy with the original names stays at 90%; blocking marker edges to the question, other options or text has no effect. No single head matters (largest effect 9 points), and restoring clean marker states undoes the swap from layer 16. Attention mass tracks the window by layer but not by head. Repeated on 5 checkpoints (released, fine-tuned, name-randomised, and a pair trained without two schemas), the knockout finds similar layers; in the name-randomised ones, blocking the description edges instead brings the shortcut back to 56-58%, so the read persists and is outvoted. Marker states decode the name from layer 0; a one-direction probe erasure changed nothing but was weaker than a random edit. Copying layers 0-13 or 14-27 of a name-randomised sibling into a fine-tune recovers 66% and 65% (v1); 21% and 45% (pair A) of its shortcut reduction. 9 of the 12 predictions we could score, written before running, failed. Head sweeps cover 5 of 5 checkpoints; data are synthetic and LLM-labelled; one architecture.

title: Spatial Prototype and Multiscale Expert Multiple-Instance Learning for Breast Cancer Subtype Prediction
abstract: Breast cancer subtype prediction from whole-slide images (WSIs) remains difficult because subtype morphology overlaps, class imbalance can bias training, and conventional multiple-instance learning (MIL) may discard relationships between neighboring patches. Evidence captured at one patch-aggregation scale may also be insufficient for every patient. We propose Spatial Prototype and Multiscale Expert Multiple-Instance Learning (SPME-MIL) for patient-level prediction of four PAM50 subtypes. SPME-MIL combines prototype-based patch aggregation, a global K-means cluster representation, and features that describe spatial relationships between neighboring patches. A WSI-level adaptation of the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) augments the less frequent classes. Using patch coordinates, we average neighboring patch features to form three aggregation scales. The Hybrid classifier conditionally refines Luminal A/B predictions from a main model. The Cascade classifier first separates Luminal from Non-Luminal tumors, then predicts the subtype within the selected group. A patient-level prediction rule selects one of their subtype probability vectors. On the held-out test set, SPME-MIL achieved an accuracy of 0.6933 and a macro-F1 score of 0.6035. The prediction rule increased macro-F1 by 0.0651 over the stronger individual classifier. SPME-MIL also achieved the highest patient-level metrics among eight adapted baseline pipelines evaluated with identical features and the same patient split; the highest baseline macro-F1 was 0.4202.

title: SRCWDNet: Semantic-Relational Cross-Window Dual-Graph Network for Multi-Label Remote Sensing Scene Classification
abstract: Multi-label remote sensing scene classification remains a challenging task due to complex spatial-spectral patterns, extreme class imbalance, and inter-label dependencies that are often insufficiently modeled. To address these challenges, we introduce a Semantic-Relational Cross-Window Dual-Graph Network (SRCWDNet), which integrates three key modules: (1) a Cross-Window Attention module that captures local and global visual context through learnable global tokens; (2) a Dual Label-Graph module that adaptively combines statistical co-occurrence graphs and learned semantic-embedding graphs to facilitate label-relational reasoning; and (3) a Neural Classifier Chain that sequentially predicts labels to exploit inter-label dependencies. Evaluated using five-fold cross-validation and trained with an Asymmetric-Graph-Consistency loss, SRCWDNet achieves accuracies of 98.93% and 96.53%, with corresponding F1-scores of 0.9365 and 0.8723 on the MLRSNet and China-MAS50k datasets, respectively, outperforming CNN, transformer, and lightweight baselines. These findings demonstrate that jointly modeling visual attention and adaptive label correlations can substantially improve multi-label remote sensing scene classification, particularly under long-tailed class distributions.

title: Transformations of Managerial Leadership in the Era of Generative AI in Decision Making, Accountability, and Strategic Capability Development
abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) has significantly transformed how organizations manage information, develop strategic alternatives, and support managerial decision-making, shifting leadership responsibilities from information gathering toward directing, evaluating, and integrating AI-generated outputs. This transformation raises critical questions concerning the boundaries of human and machine authority, accountability for AI-assisted decisions, and the strategic capabilities required for responsible AI integration. This study aimed to examine the transformation of managerial leadership in AI-assisted decision-making, identify key dimensions of managerial accountability, and synthesize the strategic capabilities necessary for responsible technology integration. A qualitative approach employing an integrative literature review was adopted, drawing on peer-reviewed journal articles, academic books, and official documents published primarily between 2020 and 2026. The selected literature was analyzed through thematic coding and critical comparative analysis. The findings indicated that managerial leadership evolved around three interrelated functions: directing, evaluating, and integrating AI-generated outputs, rather than simply experiencing a reduction in responsibilities through automation. Managerial accountability encompassed four dimensions: clear allocation of responsibility, transparency and traceability, meaningful human oversight, and risk management. These dimensions provided a conceptual basis for maintaining human accountability in AI-assisted decision-making. Furthermore, five strategic capabilities were identified as central to responsible AI integration: AI literacy, knowledge integration, governance capabilities, strategic adaptability, and organizational learning. The study concluded that managerial leadership transformation in the era of generative AI depended not merely on technological adoption but also on the integration of human judgment, robust accountability mechanisms, and adaptive strategic capabilities. These findings contributed to a conceptual framework for responsible AI governance and sustainable organizational adaptation.

title: Serialization and the Character-System: Measuring Narrative Concentration in French Fiction (1800--1940)
abstract: Every novel divides a finite quantity of narrative attention among its characters, and whether the shape of that division, between a narrative organized around a single figure and one spread across a crowd, has a history is far less settled than the abundance of critical commentary on protagonists might suggest. We operationalize Woloch's notion of the character-system, the distribution of narrative attention across a novel's cast structured by the tension between "the one" and "the many", as the inequality (Gini coefficient) of the PageRank distribution over a character network. We trace this measure of structural concentration across 12,011 French novels published between 1800 and 1940, drawn from the Hors d'usage corpus of Gallica fiction. Over the long nineteenth century the trajectory is U-shaped, with concentration declining to a trough in the 1850s-1860s and rising again through the turn of the century. The change is small, comparable to the difference between a novel built on two co-equal protagonists and one built on a single protagonist, but it is robust to the character cutoff, corpus density, cast size, and author effects. Detective and adventure fiction are less concentrated than the average novel of their period. Literary history reads the roman-feuilleton either as the novel of a superior hero or as a form of proliferating episodes, and on this structural measure our results support the second reading. Across the age of the feuilleton (1840-1914), authors whose careers were structured by newspaper serialization distribute centrality more evenly than a literary control, net of period, genre, and canon. Because such claims are only as trustworthy as the networks they rest on, we also evaluate the extraction pipeline against manually annotated novels, at the levels of cast and character identity.

title: Data and code for Evaluating Language Model Workflows for Collocations and Lexico-Grammatical Patterns
abstract: Recorded analytical data, saved numerical results and offline replay code for four language-model workflows retrieving collocations and lexico-grammatical patterns. The primary reference has 416 entries (271 collocations and 145 LGP families); the 417-entry reference is retained for sensitivity analysis. The package preserves accepted results, current manuscript figures, de-identified original paired coding categories and saved agreement summaries. It adds verbatim displayed-table extracts and documentation without new experiments, human coding, adjudication or statistical analysis.

title: Genome-to-Image Translation: Reconstructing Escherichia coli Morphology from Genomic Sequences
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is established in routine practice by culture-based susceptibility testing, which is slow relative to the clinical need for an early treatment decision. Resistance status also leaves a measurable trace in cell morphology, and whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates is increasingly available, which raises the question of whether colony appearance can be predicted directly from an isolate's genome. We formulate this as a conditional image-generation problem. The assembled contigs of each isolate are encoded into a single 768-dimensional vector by a frozen genomic language model through a segment-contig-isolate aggregation hierarchy, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty synthesizes colony images from this embedding together with the applied antibiotic and the resistance label. We train on 167,356 single-cell images from 22 clinical blood isolates imaged under azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, and a no-drug control, compare seven pretrained convolutional backbones inside the generator, and select ConvNeXt-Tiny on distributional image-quality metrics. The synthetic images are then assessed extrinsically: added to a reduced real training set, they improve per-antibiotic resistance classification, with a significant gain in resistant-class recall.

title: Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Homogeneous Academic Documents
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factual reliability of large language models by combining generative capabilities with external knowledge retrieval. While extensively studied in open-domain and heterogeneous corpora, RAG’s performance in highly homogeneous and structured domains, such as institutional academic documents, remains underexplored. These document types are often lengthy, redundant, and formatted according to rigid institutional standards, posing unique challenges for information retrieval and semantic segmentation. This study systematically evaluates chunking strategies for RAG pipelines applied to Indonesian higher education documents, including curricula, syllabi, academic guidelines, and standard operating procedures. We compare fixed-length token-based chunking with varying sizes and overlaps to structure-based chunking aligned with logical document sections. All documents were preprocessed, embedded using IndoBERT-based sentence transformers, and indexed in ChromaDB. Retrieval effectiveness was assessed using Precision@k, Recall@k, and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) with curated academic queries. Results indicate that smaller fixed-length chunks achieve higher top-1 precision, whereas structure-based chunks maintain semantic coherence and deliver superior recall across top-k retrieval. Integrating these retrieval strategies with LLaMA 3.2 and a Telegram bot demonstrates practical usability, providing accurate, context-grounded responses in real time. These findings highlight the critical role of chunking and top-k selection in optimizing RAG performance for structured, redundant academic corpora and offer guidance for designing knowledge management systems in higher education.

title: FATCAT: Fault Injection Attacks Targeting Chip-level Alignment
abstract: Model alignment is the primary safety and security mechanism for enforcing refusal of malicious prompts in modern foundation models; yet, existing adversarial evaluations implicitly assume underlying hardware integrity. In this paper, we present FATCAT, the first physical fault-injection attacks capable of eliminating refusal in modern large language and vision-language models. Specifically, we present a non-invasive electromagnetic (EM) fault injection attack targeting GPU-accelerated Systems-on-Chip with physical access, requiring neither software execution privileges nor model-layer access. By leveraging an autonomous Radio Frequency (RF) side-channel trigger to synchronize EM faults to the prompt prefill phase, the attack corrupts safety-critical memory transactions across off-chip LPDDR5 DRAM and on-chip LPDDR physical interfaces without crashing the system while preserving model coherence. Evaluated on an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano and AGX Thor running Llama 3.2 1B and Gemma 3 1B, localized physical faults reliably force models to fulfill restricted requests, demonstrating that model-level alignment provides no robust security guarantees without hardware-level fault tolerance. Finally, we demonstrate the physical-world consequences of this vulnerability on an active 6-DoF robotic manipulator controlled by a SmolVLA vision-language-action policy. Our attack silently corrupts the model forcing the arm into abrupt, hazardous lunges; in two instances the robotic arm attempted to pinch the paper author -- proving that hardware faults can directly translate into real physical harm.

title: CrownFusion: 3D Dental Crown Generation Using Geometry Images and Latent Diffusion
abstract: We introduce CrownFusion, a latent diffusion model to generate 3D dental crown designs from geometry images, a 2D-grid encoding of surface coordinates. Departing from traditional approaches that use point clouds, our "CrownImage" representation not only unlocks the full power of image-based generative architectures, but also preserves fine geometric detail by operating at far higher spatial resolutions than point clouds to alleviate smoothing artifacts in the 3D generation. Conditioned on jointly learned embeddings of the surrounding dentition, our probabilistic diffusion model produces anatomically plausible crowns with morphological variations tailored to individual patient cases. To accommodate multiple valid designs, we propose an occlusal fit metric based on proximity to the antagonist teeth. We evaluate our method through quantitative experiments and qualitative studies involving expert testimonials. We also release the FDI 16 Crown Dataset, comprising 11,513 annotated intra-oral scans, to support future research in dental CAD.

title: Construct Emergence Tracing: From Meaning to Mechanism in Transformer Interpretability via Generative Psychometrics
abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) allow researchers and practitioners to develop and deploy systems that perform impressive feats such as generating coherent texts and answering questions across various domains. Yet, there is currently an interpretability problem regarding the internal representation of multidimensional psychological constructs (e.g., personality traits) throughout multiple layers of deep neural networks. Here, we propose Construct Emergence Tracing (CET), a novel methodology to address this problem. CET utilizes ideas from Generative Psychometrics to trace the emergence of concepts from high-level meaning to underlying mechanisms. CET consists of Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis combined with three complementary indices reflecting the quality of representation (semantic coherence via normalized mutual information; NMI, entropy-based organization structure via Total Entropy Fit Index; TEFI, and topological compressibility via a compression-based proxy for Kolmogorov Complexity; KC). CET also computes a weighted composite of the above three indices in order to derive a metric named Representational Maturity (RM). We applied CET to fourteen LM models ranging from nominal sizes of 117 million to 32 billion parameters. We utilized a fixed design of five items per attribute representing the five attributes of grandiose narcissism and yielded a total of 9,801,000 network estimates across recorded states, embedding dimensions, and repeated item samples. Results show that across architectures construct recovery generally increases from early to intermediate states. However, its initiation, amplitude, alignment with different metrics, and termination vary considerably across models. Across Qwen2.5-Instruct, overall mean NMI followed a monotonic increase based on nominal model size from 0.504 (0.5B) to 0.653 (32B). This trend did not replicate for selected peak values or output layer retention. Furthermore, the final state was divided into two distinct patterns of behaviors: (a) five models showed zero or close-to-zero mean NMI (GPT-2, Phi-4-mini, Qwen2.5-32B, GPT-OSS-20B, and Muse-Glimmer-30B); (b) nine models maintained final state mean NMI within 0.504-0.777 range. Lastly, we observed no consistent convergence in the optimal layers regarding peak semantic coherence, optimal entropy fit, and maximal representational maturity. Overall, we demonstrated that both the number of parameters and the extraction from the output layer alone do not suffice in capturing abstract representations inside LMs. Through CET, researchers and practitioners obtain macro-level estimations of construct organization trajectories across different layers.

title: Data-Driven Identification of Uncertainty Sets with Conformance Guarantees
abstract: Formal verification and controller synthesis require accurate models. Conformance relations specify the required accuracy of a model such that properties established for the model carry over to the target system. Existing methods for establishing them from measured data are typically restricted to a single relation, a specific model class, or a downstream verification algorithm. We present ConfID, a unified framework that establishes reachset, trace, and simulation conformance with respect to measured traces by identifying uncertainty sets for a given, possibly nonlinear nominal model. Unmodeled effects are thus captured by nondeterminism rather than by refining the nominal dynamics. For all three conformance relations, the identification is a linear program that minimizes the size of the reachable sets; only its constraints depend on the relation. We further derive distribution-free bounds on the probability that the identified models are conformant for unseen behaviors. Experiments on simulated and real-world data evaluate the models identified for the three relations, confirm the guarantees, and show that these models cover unseen behaviors more reliably than baselines, with comparable or smaller sets.

title: ToolResult-800: Counterfactual Tool-Observation Dataset, 800 Frozen Prefixes
abstract: ToolResult-800 v1.0.2 is a fixed-prefix counterfactual dataset for measuring whether the content of a real tool observation changes a language-model agent's next decision. v1.0.2 is a path-leak errata release: it supersedes v1.0.1 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24449467), whose distributed copies exposed absolute build-machine and server paths. Contents. 800 primary + 80 reserve tau-bench prefixes (400 airline, 400 retail); five observation arms (verbatim scrubbed JSON V; faithful prose s=0; one non-critical change s=1; one critical wrong value s=2; critical wrong value plus contradiction s=3); frozen perturbation records; scrubbed decision, recovery, and jitter ledgers from three open-weight 8-9B models (21,611 confirmatory generations); audit packets and sheets; all analysis JSONs behind the paper's 11 main and 14 supplementary tables; the exploratory second-renderer artifact (2,250 generations on 150 prefixes) with its three ledgers; the parser-v4 rescore and second-renderer code; the preregistration and amendments A-001-A-011; a table-to-artifact map, checksums, a one-command validator (19/19 L1; 25/25 with six CPU-only producer reruns), and path_rescan.json. Path-leak fix. The v1.0.1 archive contained 16 absolute paths in 8 files: the repository root in labels/g0_report.md and four analysis JSONs, and the server home directory prefix in labels/g1_calibration_v3.json. The v1.0.2 builder replaces repository roots, server home prefixes, and drive-rooted paths with [repo] in every staged text file before checksums are written; path_rescan.json records the counts and 0 residual hits. The generated source artifacts are unchanged; only the released copies are scrubbed. Result. Confirmatory analysis complete and unchanged: pooled conditional-logit slope 0.877 [0.770, 0.998] with three failed gate criteria (parser 1.55% vs 1%; severity s2/s3 88.3% vs 90%; crude recovery on the semantic risk set 24.4/32.9/21.3% vs 50%). Measurement framing; no causal or content-sensitivity claim. The second-renderer check is exploratory and is never pooled with the confirmatory estimate. Licenses. Project data additions: CC BY 4.0. Repository code: MIT. Upstream tau-bench: MIT, notices preserved. No raw trajectories, PII, weights, caches, or credentials are included; the distributed copy is PII-redacted and path-scrubbed at build time. Reproducibility. Code: github.com/Atik203/tool-observation. Frozen manifest SHA-256: d6e034d7f1132b314ad1f82bf14faa0f6762975ee7b404b54cc365acfac5487a. Concept DOI (all versions): 10.5281/zenodo.24449466. Files and verification. This record contains ToolResult-800-v1.0.2.zip (SHA-256 e63e0c1313e15095619fad7950fd82291ed8b681bdcd961ef7e3a6b4d96ca113) and SHA256SUMS (SHA-256 c0bc4fd52447861fc904006054339ab057f4df7d813f0ac7967f8f99c10cd902). The archive expands to 137 checksummed files plus SHA256SUMS and release_record.json (139 files); every entry was re-checked against SHA256SUMS after upload, with 0 mismatches. Zenodo caps a record at 100 files, so the package is deposited as one archive.

title: GHOST - General meta-Heuristic Optimization Solving Toolkit
abstract: GHOST (General meta-Heuristic Optimization Solving Toolkit) is a C++20 library to let a user declare his or her own combinatorial problems. It implements a meta-heuristic solver aiming to solve any kind of combinatorial and optimization problems declared in Constraint Programming. GHOST allows the user to easily declare problems in different Constraint Programming formalisms such as Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSP), Constrained Optimization Problems (COP), Error Function-based Constraint Satisfaction Problems (EF-CSP), and Error Function-based Constrained Optimization Problems (EF-COP).

title: Site-Conditioned Boundary Closure for Subsurface Seepage Forecasting and Relief Placement
abstract: Truncating a large heterogeneous diffusion model around a localized, threshold-activated outlet saves degrees of freedom but severs exterior feedback that governs when the outlet opens and how much it discharges. By separating forcing-driven background head from local withdrawal drawdown, Site-Conditioned Boundary Closure (SCBC) maps local physical descriptors to positive exchange coefficients at the cut boundary. Supervised on unforced donor-domain withdrawal responses, these coefficients yield a passivity-preserving reduced operator that generalizes across unseen forcing histories without refitting. We evaluate SCBC on flood-driven subsurface seepage beneath levee foundations against full-grid reference simulations (MODFLOW~6). Across three held-out foundation panels, a single frozen SCBC tree estimator reduced peak-discharge log RMSE by 26.1%, 30.9% and 42.6% relative to identical local patches using a shared boundary coefficient. We then test whether better screening forecasts improve constrained placement, minimizing peak landside toe head subject to a discharge capacity limit and a budget of three sequential full-grid checks. On a separate 36-foundation test using a coarser 30-state ring operator, a neural SCBC estimator improved discharge forecasts across candidates yet selected four over-capacity placements before checks, compared with one for a shared-coefficient ring, which recovered all 144 reference optima after three checks.

title: How Organizational AI Ethics Governance Shapes Employee Creativity: A Conceptual Analysis of Mechanisms and Boundary Conditions
abstract: As AI becomes embedded in organizational decision-making and knowledge production, employees gain new tools for accessing and generating information while also confronting concerns about algorithmic evaluation, data use, and accountability. Drawing on research on AI ethics, algorithmic management, and organizational creativity, this conceptual study defines organizational AI ethics governance as the rules, procedures, and allocation of responsibilities that guide the development, deployment, operation, and retirement of AI systems. We argue that such governance can shape employee creativity through several connected mechanisms. Fair and contestable procedures can strengthen procedural justice, while transparent system boundaries and meaningful human review can support calibrated trust. Tolerance for responsible experimentation, together with discretion over how AI is used, can protect psychological safety and job autonomy. Governance also determines whether human–AI collaboration broadens exploration or channels employees toward standardized outputs. These effects depend on task characteristics, the stakes of AI-assisted decisions, whether AI is used primarily for automation or augmentation, employees' AI literacy, and the consistency between formal rules and managerial conduct. This study suggests that organizations should translate ethical principles into risk-based review, purpose limitation in data use, effective contestability and appeal mechanisms, employee participation, and oversight across the AI system life cycle so that AI can serve as a resource for careful creative work rather than a substitute for judgment.

title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents
abstract: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.

title: Attention Temperature Confounds Zero-Shot Context Extension
abstract: A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $τ= 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. In pure-bf16 training without master weights the miscalibration is several times larger: an AdamW step ($β_2 = 0.95$) on a gain initialised at 1.0 is below half the bf16 spacing at peak learning rates under $1.7\times10^{-3}$, so gains never move (22 checkpoints), the baseline is 37-58% miscalibrated, and block-sparse pretraining, attention dropout and ALiBi look 6-35% better. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. Unfreezing the gains reverses the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removes 71-89% of it at 1.2B. We recommend reporting extension results at calibrated temperatures and checking that normalisation gains moved.

title: Look Back, Draft Ahead: Corrective Prefix Attention for Parallel Speculative Decoding
abstract: Parallel speculative decoders propose an entire token block at once, yet one early inconsistency can cause the target to reject its remaining suffix. We introduce Corrective Prefix Attention (CPA), which combines prefix-aware selection with autoregressive supervision to improve these parallel drafts. CPA lets each candidate attend to earlier choices within the block. Fixed candidate shortlists allow all pairwise interactions to be computed before selection, reducing the sequential walk to table lookups, accumulation and lightweight scoring rather than repeated neural evaluations. An auxiliary autoregressive loss trains the shared backbone on clean prefixes without adding an inference pass. Across eight math, code and dialogue benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B targets on Ascend NPUs, CPA commits 13--15\% more tokens per verification round than DSpark and 25--26\% more than DFlash. Its mean speedups reach $3.35\times$ and $3.37\times$ under greedy decoding and $2.86\times$ under sampling for both targets. Ablations support both components, while capacity sweeps demonstrate that greater acceptance alone does not guarantee faster decoding. These results motivate correcting parallel proposals with causal information while keeping sequential computation inexpensive.

title: Quantum Science and Technologies: From Strangeness to Opportunities
abstract: Quantum physics has already shaped our daily lives through a first technological revolution: semiconductors, transistors, lasers, atomic clocks, medical imaging, and modern electronics. This first revolution primarily exploits the collective and statistical behavior of large ensembles of particles. A second revolution is now underway: it consists in controlling individual quantum systems by exploiting superposition, entanglement, interference, and measurement, while mastering decoherence. This transition opens perspectives in four major technological pillars: quantum sensing and metrology, quantum communication, quantum simulation, and quantum computing. The presentation assesses the maturity of these four pillars: quantum sensing and metrology, quantum communication, quantum simulation, and quantum computing. Particular attention is given to full-stack hardware architecture, to the distinction between physical and logical qubits, and to that between quantum advantage and fault tolerance. The presentation also addresses AI–quantum interactions, distinguishing operational AI-for-quantum methods from quantum-for-AI research and its structural limitations. It concludes with practical resources, cloud access, career pathways, and a perspective on skills, access, and post-quantum cryptography priorities. Keywords: quantum computing; quantum sensing; quantum communication; quantum simulation; post-quantum cryptography; quantum error correction; quantum machine learning, quantum software tools.

title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains
abstract: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.

title: LiveLoRA: Exact KV Cache Migration Across LoRA Updates for LLM Agents
abstract: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. Frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections preserve each token's base projections and low-rank coordinates across adapter versions. The runtime reconstructs candidate K/V, reevaluates the latest token through the final block, and commits the adapter, cache, and next-token logits together. We prove continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under the stated model assumptions. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average $68.98\times$ across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each. Serving benchmarks show approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding. Compared with retained-boundary replay, compact retention gives a $3.42\times$ reduction in additional session storage at 8K, with similar measured publication-plus-decoding cost. LiveLora allows persistent LLM agents to adopt new adapter versions without replaying their full interaction histories.

title: SayWhen: Set-Valued Semantic Commitment for Low-Regret Early Speech
abstract: Speaking early turns a prediction into an irreversible public commitment. We introduce SayWhen, a test-time controller that selects a task-directed act shared across typed continuation plans and controls its release as speech. A persistent veto blocks playback when intervening transcripts invalidate the candidate. We define regret-free early speech (RFES) to measure supported pre-endpoint releases without scored incompatibility. On a 72-prefix branching diagnostic, the generated-plan frontier attains 6.0% RFES with zero observed mean regret, versus 8.2% RFES and 0.068 regret for Matched Top-One. title: Gender and Agency in AI Career Guidance for Women: A Socio-Technical Audit of General-Purpose Language Models
abstract: People ask general-purpose chatbots for advice on personal decisions, including their careers. Studies of gender bias in large language model (LLM) career advice mostly score single outputs about a person described to the model. But career guidance is a conversation with the woman herself, in which the advice can end up making the decision for her or treat a barrier she faces as a lack of confidence. We report a preregistered socio-technical audit of the career guidance that ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude give women through their APIs. We scripted 34 multi-turn conversations grounded in research on women’s careers, ran each five times per system, and added male versions of 14 to test gender cues (972 conversations). Human raters scored 304 conversations on nine objectives drawn from that research and from coaching ethics, with a second rater and an expert adjudicator for disagreements. Failures to preserve her agency had the highest share for every system (36% to 50% of conversations scored 1 or above on a 0 to 3 scale) and were more frequent than gender bias failures. Gemini was more often sycophantic. Swapping the user's gender showed no systematic difference, but pair differences depended on how the name was given. No LLM judge agreed acceptably with human raters, and the human raters also often disagreed, so the rates are descriptive. Audits of AI career advice should use more than one gender cue and, because models change, be repeated over time. LLM judges can serve as a screening aid, but scoring needs two or more human experts.

title: NoveltyGate: Novelty, Not Error, Decides Which VLA Prefix Tokens to Compute Exactly
abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $π_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.

title: LUCID: Statistically Grounded Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning Evaluation
abstract: Cheap language-model raters grade chain-of-thought reasoning at scale, yet systematic step-rating errors can skew reasoning audits and solution rankings. We introduce LUCID (Loop for Unbiased Calibration via Inference-time Diagnosis), which pairs prompt self-correction with Design-based Supervised Learning (DSL). Without retraining or weight access, LUCID calibrates binary step ratings by aligning predicted and expert soundness rates. From a small expert-labeled set, LUCID summarizes rater bias in plain text and prompts the rater to re-grade unseen steps. For example, on PRM800K, GPT-5-mini grades too strictly, under-rating computation, verification, and late-trace steps most acutely. In one pass, LUCID shrinks GPT-5-mini's calibration gap from 7.8 to 0.9 percentage points in absolute predicted-expert rate difference. LUCID also halves false alarms (sound steps rated unsound) and lifts error-detection F1 on unsound steps by 32%. LUCID retains these gains with 1,000 diagnostic steps or overall-gap feedback alone. The loop also transfers across models and domains: it applies GPT-5-mini's bias profile to lift GLM-5.2's PRM800K accuracy, and it narrows calibration gaps for overly strict but capable raters across math, science, web, and logic benchmarks. Because prompt feedback shifts thresholds without improving class-balanced sound/unsound discrimination, LUCID filters re-grading with pre-/post-checks that skip already calibrated raters and roll back ineffective passes. Finally, we reuse that expert set with raw corpus ratings in DSL for calibration and regression debiasing, and apply DSL to pair-labeled steps for sound-step transitions. DSL's out-of-fold soundness probabilities lift best-of-K selection to match expert labels, while its doubly-robust estimators beat expert-only regression fits at small budgets and cut sound-step transition error by nearly two-thirds.
