title: RumiFold: Teaching an LLM to Natively Fold Proteins and Reason About Their Function
abstract: Can we teach a general-purpose language model to fold proteins? And if so, what does learning to fold enable beyond structure prediction itself? We introduce RumiFold, a pretrained chat model that learns to predict protein structures directly from its own hidden states. RumiFold processes proteins through repeated folding passes, then uses these folded representations to answer questions in natural language. It achieves folding accuracy comparable to dedicated single-representation models such as SimpleFold, alongside state-of-the-art performance on Gene Ontology protein function prediction and free-text function description. We find that folding pretraining organizes the model's hidden states around protein function, creating an internal per-residue workspace that is biologically grounded. Causal interventions show that this folded workspace links structure and language when RumiFold predicts function, providing rich representations for biomolecular reasoning. We see RumiFold as a step toward native biomolecular intelligence: where protein-based computations and language-based reasoning become integrated capabilities of general-purpose language models. Code, data, and models are available at: https://rumifold.baulab.info

title: MSBench: Benchmarking Script-Controlled Multi-Shot Text-to-Video Generation
abstract: Text-to-video (T2V) models can now generate visually plausible short clips, but multi-shot generation requires a different set of skills: composing multiple shots with intended cut timing, transition style, camera language, and cross-shot continuity. How far this multi-shot output can be controlled from text remains unmeasured: existing benchmarks either evaluate single shots or, when they provide shot-level scripts, typically check whether the requested shots appear but not when they change or how they are joined. We introduce MSBench, a benchmark for controllable text-driven multi-shot video generation built around structured Scene-Entity-Shot mini-scripts that specify each shot's time span, camera state, content, and outgoing transition. MSBench defines a four-dimensional hybrid evaluation framework spanning Visual Quality, Dynamic Quality, Semantic Alignment, and Cross-Shot Consistency with 11 sub-metrics. Experiments on 14 commercial and open-source systems show that visual quality does little to separate the systems, whereas multi-shot control does: many models cut mainly on scene changes and render requested gradual transitions as hard cuts. Human evaluations further validate MSBench, with its system ranking reaching a Spearman correlation of 0.87 with human preferences. The project page is available at https://totalhuang.github.io/MSBench-page/.

title: PINE: Point, Instance and Normal Estimation in One-Step Diffusion Model
abstract: Understanding a scene requires both geometry and semantics: geometry recovers its spatial structure, and semantics separates it into objects. Current models obtain the two from separate networks or separate passes. We present PINE, a one-step Omni Diffusion Transformer that predicts the point map, the surface normals, and the instance map of an image in one forward pass. PINE treats each map as a token stream, and a stream mask decides which streams interact. A camera-aware ray encoding positions every token by its camera ray rather than its pixel. Grounding attention adds the affinity of pretrained DINOv3 features to the attention logits. Trained on only 139K synthetic images for geometry, PINE achieves state-of-the-art point maps whether or not intrinsics are given and the best average rank on surface normals. It also exceeds SAM on large objects with less than 1 percent of its training images, and it predicts all three maps 5.7x faster than MoGe-3 with SAM.

title: MusicListenBench: Can Audio LLMs Hear the Difference Yet?
abstract: Audio large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on song genre, mood, and instrumentation. A more basic skill is telling whether two short clips play the same melody, chord or instrument. We introduce MusicListenBench, a benchmark of paired listening tests for melody, harmony, timbre, and tempo. Each test item comes with two variants. A FLIP variant changes the music, so the answer must change. A STAY variant changes only the sound, such as room echo or hiss, so the answer must stay the same. The two variants have opposite answers, so a model that ignores the audio scores 50%, whatever letter it prefers. The benchmark has a training split and two test sets, one rendered from symbolic music with exact labels and one built from real recordings. On the rendered test, seven of eight open audio LLMs score within 4 points of this floor. Of four commercial models, both GPT-Audio models are at chance, and the best, Gemini 2.5 Pro, reaches 74.2%, 12.8 points below human listeners (87.0%). Post-training with GRPO on 10k rendered clean pairs raises Qwen2.5-Omni from 61.2% to 99.0% on held-out clean pairs, and the gain transfers to a task left out of training. On FLIP/STAY, however, it only reaches the level of our listeners (86.0%). It now misses almost no change (1.9%, against 24.7% for Gemini 2.5 Pro), yet when only the sound changes, it turns a correct answer into a wrong one 25.7\% of the time. More than half of its false flips come from a quiet background hiss. Models learn to hear a difference much faster than they learn which differences matter. On real recordings, open models again stay near chance, and the trained model calls 27 of 42 pairs of two strums of the same chord different. Adding sound-only pairs to training lowers false flips on both test sets, but no training run teaches relative pitch. We release the data, code, and an open leaderboard.

title: Beyond Attention Maps: Understanding and Improving Medical MLLMs via Visual Values
abstract: Current MLLM methods largely focus on whether models attend to the right visual regions, implicitly treating spatial attention map as the primary key of effective visual perception. To examine this assumption, we introduce a medical VQA dataset with paired non-contrast (NC) and contrast-enhanced (CE) images that share corresponding anatomy while providing different cues. We show that this view is incomplete: across paired NC and CE medical images, MLLMs often exhibit similar attention patterns despite producing contrasting answers, while controlled bidirectional interventions induce substantially larger prediction changes on visual values than attention weights. These results identify the visual content retrieved through values as a critical factor in improving perception beyond spatial attention alone. Guided by this finding, we propose VIVID (VIsual Value Intervention Distillation), which uses enhanced visual values to identify and refine teacher corrections aligned with useful visual evidence to improve on-policy distillation from CE to NC images. Across six internal and external test sets, VIVID consistently outperforms existing on-policy distillation methods across different model scales and architectures, requires only NC images at inference, and maintains strong zero-shot performance on general-domain VQA benchmarks. The project page is available at https://qiuzyc.github.io/VIVID.

title: Polytropos: What Do Vision-Language Model Descriptions Make of a Cultural Object?
abstract: Vision-language models have become a new kind of describer, writing about almost anything people see, and their descriptions now shape how cultures are known by people and by other models. Descriptions of cultures tend to turn particular things into types, and what a description loses shows what its describer lacks. We introduce Polytropos, a benchmark that measures what model descriptions of cultural objects keep of the particular object by turning each description back into an image and comparing it with the original photograph. On 374 objects from the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Getty, with 1,870 descriptions from five models and 230 written by curators, reconstructions are recognised as the recorded culture more often than the photographs, at 54.55% to 59.09% against 52.14%, yet 16% to 21% of objects change outcome and only 0.49% of reconstructions are identified as the specific object. On the same objects, models lose recorded cultures at a rate similar to curators but gain more. Model descriptions give each object many faces, each typical of its culture and almost none the object itself.

title: Deterministic Office Document Fabrication
abstract: This paper describes a workflow for producing and reviewing editable office documents with AI agents. Synthetic Word, Excel, and PowerPoint cases separate checks for document structure, calculation dependencies, and presentation claims. Application-level checks document bounded observations under a named Office build. The paper does not estimate comparative productivity or learner outcomes.

title: A Glimpse of Training VLMs as Foundation Models for Robotic Manipulation
abstract: Recently, GPT-6 Astra demonstrates strong generalization in robot control, yet limited disclosure of its training leaves open how such capabilities can be reproduced. We introduce nanoAstra, an approach to training vision-language models (VLMs) for generalizable manipulation that combines semantic action modeling with capability-preserving supervised fine-tuning (CP-SFT). nanoAstra represents robot behavior as semantic steps composed of reusable, parameterized action primitives, guided by explicit progress descriptions. Meanwhile, CP-SFT uses an explicit robot-specific system prompt to constrain manipulation outputs to a structured action space, aiming to focus adaptation on robot-specific contexts and promote specialization while minimizing interference with broader pretrained capabilities. With this formulation, we train nanoAstra on more than 5,000 hours of robot data together with general VQA data. On RoboTwin 2.0's randomized benchmark, nanoAstra-9B achieves a 17.8% zero-shot success rate, substantially outperforming advanced VLA and WAM baselines as well as similarly sized VLMs. With inference faster than the corresponding motion execution on a single H20 GPU, our model supports action-chunk-like streaming execution that overlaps inference with motion, reducing the robot's idle time from 35.0% to 6.9%.

title: MODAL-ORGANIZATIONAL MODEL OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
abstract: This document presents a self-contained formal specification of the Modal-Organizational Model of Artificial Intelligence (MOTAI), a conceptual framework for representing cognitive capabilities as properties of computational organizations rather than isolated elementary components.The model characterizes an artificial system through its internal states, available operators, admissible programs, organizational constraints, and resource costs. These components determine which transformations the system can realize and which tasks it can perform under specified conditions.Three categories are formally distinguished: actualized operations, operationally accessible capabilities, and transformationally accessible capabilities. The third category includes functions that become available through explicitly permitted changes to the organization itself.The specification introduces resource-bounded compositional closure, task-grounded capability sets, modal capability profiles, relations of functional dominance, and constrained organizational transformations.Seven formal results establish properties of the model, including monotonicity under resource expansion, invariance under structure-preserving recoding, limitations of restricted behavioral equivalence, conservativity of definable operator extensions, resource-sensitive capability expansion, preservation of existing capabilities under optional transformations, and the existence of incomparable capability profiles.Two worked examples illustrate the distinction between compositional expansion and computational efficiency.The framework is compatible with established traditions in causal abstraction, compositional computation, functionalism, and computational theory. It does not claim that its elementary propositions constitute previously unknown mathematical theorems.Its intended contribution is the integration of these formal structures into a coherent model for distinguishing realized computation, available function, organizational constraints, and transformations of cognitive possibility.No original empirical investigation is conducted. The specification is intended for theoretical analysis, philosophical comparison, subsequent mathematical refinement, and independent reuse.

title: ζ_0: A Framework for World Action Models with Joint Scene and Body Foresight in Humanoid Control
abstract: World Action Models anticipate visual outcomes to guide robot actions, yet humanoid interaction also depends on how the robot's body responds. Visual foresight alone can miss body motion, while latent-distance losses do not directly supervise action responses. We present ζ_0, a framework that turns vision-language-action policies into World Action Models by foreseeing future visual features and measured joint trajectories in a shared latent representation. During training, a teacher conditioned on recorded futures provides a reference action response, and dual-response transfer trains the causal predictor to match it through the teacher and the executing policy. All components are trained jointly, and deployment uses only causally predicted futures. On seven HumanoidArena tasks, ζ_0 built on Ψ_0 and GR00T N1.7 reaches 63.6% and 79.5% mean success, 18.8 and 9.0 points above these bases. On six real-world tasks, it reaches 78.3% and 85.0%, gains of 16.7 and 10.0 points. On GR00T, its 79.5% tops all compared seven-task joint policies. Project page: https://chenyizhi123.github.io/zeta0-project/

title: OAT3D: A Generative Model for 3D Shape- and Resolution-Free Structural Topology Optimization
abstract: Topology optimization determines how material should be distributed within a design domain to optimize structural performance under prescribed loads, supports, and constraints. The problems are highly nonconvex, and conventional solvers require repeated finite element analyses, making high-resolution 3D topology optimization computationally expensive. Data-driven approaches face an additional bottleneck: generating training datasets requires solving large numbers of these costly problems, so existing work in data-driven topology optimization primarily focuses on 2D problems. Large-scale 3D datasets remain scarce, and existing models remain limited in problem scale and boundary-condition diversity. Here, we introduce Optimize Any Topology-3D (OAT3D), a generative model for high-resolution 3D structural topology optimization. OAT3D introduces a novel sparse problem encoding to represent load and fixity conditions and combines a sparse volumetric variational autoencoder with a conditional diffusion transformer. title: Human Intent vs. Algorithmic Density: What the Riemann Hypothesis Breakthrough Reveals About the Future of AI
abstract: Human Intent vs. Algorithmic Density: What the Riemann Hypothesis Breakthrough Reveals About the Future of AI Two days ago, the mathematical world experienced a seismic shift. Mathematician Levent Alpöge, collaborating with Anthropic’s Claude, announced a formal proof of the 167-year-old Riemann Hypothesis—one of the most famous unsolved problems in history. Instead of a traditional journal paper, the proof arrived as over 17 million lines of code in Lean, a formal verification language. Machine checkers rapidly verified the logical steps. Yet, leading mathematicians like Terence Tao immediately pointed out the real challenge ahead: humans now have to sift through this massive ocean of code to actually understand the underlying idea. On the exact same day, Italian mathematician Alessandro Masullo released a 940-page, purely human-written manuscript on the same problem—built over 12 years without a single line of AI assistance, though still containing gaps that require refinement. This historic moment highlights a fundamental tension I explored in my recent Zenodo research note ("Human Intent vs. Algorithmic Density"): the boundary between algorithmic density and human intent. Here is why these two worlds are not contradicting each other, but converging on the exact same truth: 1. Machines Provide Density; Humans Provide DirectionIn the Riemann proof, AI demonstrated breathtaking algorithmic density—the ability to brute-force, verify, and weave together millions of formal logical steps. However, it still required a human to frame the problem, set the trajectory, and now, to extract meaning from the output. In my AINUMPSA framework, I define this through the axiom 1 > 0: computation alone (0) is just infinite iteration or noise until conscious human intent (1) injects a directional vector of existence and meaning. 2. The Limit of Pure ComputabilityFormal systems like Lean tolerate zero gaps—every micro-step must be explicitly calculated. While this works brilliantly in closed logical systems, reality, physics, and physical art operate differently. In my work on Chrono-Acoustic Brane Mechanics (CABM) and physical painting (Sovereign Impasto), I call these Uncomputable Nodes—the non-linear restraints, biological feedback, and intentional gaps where true insight happens. Even in mathematics, Gödel’s incompleteness theorems remind us that mechanical rules alone cannot capture every truth without an intuitive leap from outside the system. 3. The Rise of the "Homo-Machine" HybridNeither pure computation nor unassisted human effort holds the monopoly on the future. The breakthrough in number theory and explorations in generative art and cognitive philosophy point to the same destination: a hybrid architecture. We are moving past the era of "AI replacing humans" into an era where AI acts as a high-density resonator and verification engine, while the human mind remains the sovereign observer, navigator, and source of intent. Computation can prove that something works. Only human consciousness can understand why it matters. What are your thoughts on the 17-million-line proof—is machine-verified truth enough, or does mathematics require human comprehension to be complete? #ArtificialIntelligence #Mathematics #RiemannHypothesis #FutureOfWork #HumanMachineCollaboration #PhilosophyOfAI #DeepTech

title: GameAnything: From Any Inspirations to Playable Game Worlds
abstract: AI-driven game development holds the potential to transform diverse human inspirations into interactive experiences. However, existing systems and benchmarks primarily focus on explicit development specifications, with limited support for adapting multimodal references and evaluating actual gameplay experiences. We introduce GameAnything, an open-source agentic platform that transforms multimodal inspirations into playable extensions of existing games through iterative development. GameAnything integrates coding agents with an independent playtesting critic, persistent development state, and reusable experience memory to support continuous refinement. We further present GameAnything-Bench, a benchmark spanning diverse reference modalities, game creation objectives, and gaming environments, with exploratory gameplay testing to assess both functional correctness and gameplay quality. Evaluations of nine coding agent configurations reveal that current agents can adapt reference content but still struggle with playable interactions and precise modifications. Moreover, multimodal references improve content fidelity, while iterative refinement yields substantial but varying improvements across agents. These findings highlight both the potential and remaining challenges of inspiration-driven game development.

title: Aaron Burr to Joseph Alston, July 1804 (Gilder Lehrman GLC01523, clear page): transcription, key and reading of the stroke-and-figure cipher
abstract: Supporting material for a cipher solution submitted to HistoCrypt 2027: transcription, recovered key, decoder script, reading, working notes, statistical validation and the fixed-field profile for the stroke-and-figure cipher on the clear page of Aaron Burr's letter to his son-in-law Joseph Alston, written at New York between 18 and 21 July 1804 and filed as Gilder Lehrman GLC01523 (132 cipher signs in seven lines, mixed with clear words). The cipher is a simple substitution of 21 signs (figures and hatched stroke groups) for English letters, with the words divided. The key was recovered from pattern words in the cipher itself, starting from Gilder Lehrman's transcript of the signs checked against the page image; all 132 signs read, with one word (pleant, perhaps pliant) one sign off. The letter asks, in cipher, what to do if the coroner's inquest finds murder. The reading has no external review: the authors' notes record none by a Burr specialist, and the transcription was not rechecked against the original page. Images are not included: they are the Hamilton Education Program (Gilder Lehrman Institute) page images at https://hamilton.gilderlehrman.org/supporting-document/burrs-coded-letter-about-duel-1804. Write-up: https://cyphersolver.com/burr1804.html. Source repository: https://github.com/dbourdeau/cyphersolver (folder targets/burr1804).

title: Tenlai-TTS 2.0: Continuous-Representation LLM-Based TTS System with End-to-End Training
abstract: Autoregressive text-to-speech (TTS) with continuous speech latents avoids quantization-induced information loss, but typically relies on a latent space that is learned separately and then frozen before language-model training. Such a space must satisfy two competing requirements: it must retain enough acoustic detail for high-fidelity reconstruction, yet be sufficiently structured and regularized to support autoregressive prediction by a language model. We present Tenlai-TTS 2.0, which learns continuous speech representations through end-to-end training to balance acoustic detail with autoregressive predictability. The model comprises a speech encoder with a capacity-controlled Gaussian bottleneck, a large language model (LLM) with an autoregressive diffusion transformer (AR-DiT) head, a flow-matching (FM) mel-spectrogram decoder, and a multi-task recognition model (RM). With energy normalization and fixed-variance Gaussian noise, the bottleneck has a closed-form upper bound on its information rate. Through joint optimization with reconstruction, recognition, and next-patch prediction objectives, we learn continuous speech representations that suit all three tasks and train the LLM and AR-DiT for autoregressive generation. The LLM and AR-DiT are further optimized using differentiable reconstruction and recognition feedback on their predicted latents through the FM decoder and RM. On Seed-TTS-eval, this feedback-based optimization reduces character error rate (CER) from 0.82% to 0.74% on test-zh and from 8.32% to 7.08% on test-hard-zh, and word error rate (WER) from 1.32% to 1.27% on test-en, compared with joint training alone. Subsequent reinforcement learning further reduces CER to 6.29% on test-hard-zh and WER to 1.08% on test-en, with speaker similarity scores of 0.811, 0.766, and 0.784 on test-zh, test-en, and test-hard-zh, respectively.

title: PhyCoVE: Benchmarking Physical Counterfactual Video Editing across Diverse Material Dynamics
abstract: Physical counterfactual video editing turns a source video and a language-specified physical edit at a given execution frame into a counterfactual video that shows how the scene would evolve after the edit. Existing evaluations with counterfactual target videos mainly cover object removal or specific rigid-body motions, although real scenes also involve elastic deformation, fluid flow, and interactions among rigid bodies, elastic solids, and fluids. We introduce PhyCoVE, a benchmark of 533 cases on 110 source videos that covers rigid, elastic, and fluid dynamics in five interaction patterns, with edits that remove an object, change a physical quantity, or insert a new object. For the simulated cases, a language model proposes scene designs, coding agents build them with solvers suited to each material and physically based rendering and then simulate each edit from the source scene state, and humans check every stage. For the real cases, we record continuously from one camera position before and after each edit. We also propose counterfactual fidelity, a metric that applies across materials and their interactions and measures how much of the physical change from the source video to the target video a generated video reproduces. We evaluate seven open-source and commercial video editing models and find that counterfactual fidelity ranks them nearly as human preference does, but even the best model reproduces only about one seventh of the physical change. The models change how a scene looks but rarely how it evolves, whereas a physical edit requires understanding the dynamics that it changes. Physical counterfactual video editing thus remains far from solved, and PhyCoVE provides a foundation for developing and evaluating methods for it.

title: Resampling, Stacking Diversity, and Decision Threshold Selection on Noisy Imbalanced Tabular Data
abstract: Classifying rare events in tabular datasets becomes difficult when severe class imbalance coincides with missing values, extreme outliers, and non-linear feature interactions. Under the standard 0.50 probability cutoff, classifiers often fall into the accuracy paradox: overall specificity stays high while minority cases go undetected. To examine how common remedies behave under these conditions, this study benchmarks a noisy synthetic tabular dataset (N = 3,000, 5% baseline minority weight, ~4% missing values, ~2% outliers, and ~1.5% borderline label ambiguity) strictly inside 5-fold Stratified Cross-Validation without data leakage. Across six resampling strategies (No Resampling, ROS, RUS, SMOTE, ADASYN, and SMOTE-Tomek), SMOTE-Tomek reaches the highest minority recall (0.8007) and edges out standard SMOTE on PR-AUC (0.3755 vs. 0.3748), whereas No Resampling retains the strongest PR-AUC (0.5620) and Brier Score (0.0565). Comparing single models, a tree-only stacking ensemble, and a heterogeneous stacking ensemble (Random Forest + XGBoost + Support Vector Machine with a Logistic Regression meta-learner) shows why cross-paradigm pairing helps: SVM (RBF) errors correlate far less with Random Forest (0.4934) and XGBoost (0.5661) than the two tree models correlate with each other (0.6735). That error diversity gives heterogeneous stacking the highest recall (0.8007) and well-calibrated probabilities (Brier Score = 0.0976). Finally, shifting the decision cutoff from 0.50 to Youden's J (0.0748) lifts recall from 0.5351 to 0.8007 (cutting missed detections from 126 down to 54) and raises Balanced Accuracy from 0.7203 to 0.7670.

title: Can an Agent Trust Its Own Zoom? Cross-Magnification Provenance Verification for Whole-Slide Images
abstract: Visual agents navigate whole-slide images through magnified observations associated with claimed locations. However, a visually plausible observation does not necessarily originate from its claimed location, particularly across magnifications and in regions with similar tissue structures. We formulate cross-magnification provenance verification (CMPV) to evaluate whether visual evidence supports a claimed spatial association, recover the source when possible, and abstain when evidence is insufficient. We introduce PyraFault, a benchmark of 3.06 million coordinate-supervised examples from 2,200 cases across five TCGA cohorts, covering within-context substitutions, absent-source faults, and geometric perturbations. We further propose ZoomTrace, a claim-independent verifier that estimates the observation's source before evaluating its agreement with the claimed location. It combines physical-scale alignment, visual retrieval, geometric refinement, and reliability estimation using spatially disjoint competing matches. On 503,320 test examples, ZoomTrace achieves 0.969 AUPRC and 0.987 AUROC, compared with 0.789 and 0.903 for Efficient LoFTR. Further evaluations reveal trade-offs in reliability estimation and limitations in vision-language models, cross-dataset retrieval, and calibration. Integrating ZoomTrace into visual agent tool paths reduces exposure to corrupted observations and silent failures, while downstream accuracy improvements depend on the agent and verification threshold.

title: Developing the Open Transport Ontology (OTO) as a Community Ontology
abstract: Today’s systems research is often driven by large volumes of heterogeneous data used for computational modeling and data processing. In order to make scientific results transparent and reproducible, it is necessary to share the input data, the program code, and all other parameters used to generate the results. We apply the FAIR principles to the domain of transport systems and related areas. Specifically, we develop the Open Transport Ontology used for FAIR-compliant metadata annotations. The ontology creates a data vocabulary with commonly agreed definitions of used terms and their relations to each other. This improves the interpretability of the data by using common standards to describe the data fields and allows for the inference of implicit knowledge. With this paper we introduce the Open Transport Ontology, discuss its content, and invite contributions to further development.

title: TipDex-VTLA: Learning to Refine Actions with Visual Reliability and Tactile Feedback for Dexterous Manipulation
abstract: Changes in illumination can induce action drift in dexterous manipulation even when the physical state remains unchanged. Although existing vision--tactile--language--action (VTLA) policies incorporate tactile feedback, when and how touch refines actions under changing visual conditions remains challenging. We introduce TipDex-VTLA, a VTLA policy that combines estimated visual action reliability and tactile forecast verification to regulate execution-time refinement. Specifically, Visual Action Sensitivity Estimation (VASE) learns visual reliability from a frozen reference policy's action sensitivity to illumination perturbations. Tactile Anticipation and Correction during Execution (TACE) compares predicted and measured touch at matched times and combines the resulting discrepancy with visual reliability to gate bounded feature corrections for unexecuted actions. This effectively helps to refine actions under challenging unseen visual conditions. We evaluate TipDex-VTLA on four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks and the UniVTAC simulation benchmark. TipDex-VTLA trained on data collected under normal visual conditions, achieves average full-task success rates of 87.5% (resp. 73.8%) under normal (resp. challenging unseen) lighting in real-world tasks, significantly outperforming some state-of-the-art methods. We will release the collected data and source code.

title: Exponential variance of paired determinant estimates for optical circuit readout
abstract: A shared-sign pair of determinants estimates a normalized optical-circuit acceptance probability without bias. On an explicit family of connected circuits its variance grows exponentially for every positive entry weighting fixed before sampling. Deleting any single central controlled-sign gate changes the promised decision. The proof computes the optical amplitude on the complement of alternating cycles. A second construction uses independent controls. Both decision families are classically tractable.

title: Advanced Applied AI Orchestration
abstract: This theoretical design paper describes how people can organize and revise AI-assisted work across changing execution conditions. Its execution-episode representation connects purpose, state, access, authority, allocation, handoff, checking, and recovery. Synthetic cases illustrate how changes in those conditions can lead to different decisions. The paper reports no comparative workflow or learning-effect estimate.

Synthetic cases illustrate how changes in those conditions can lead to different decisions. The paper reports no comparative workflow or learning-effect estimate.

title: Even the LLM Needs a Layer: a refusal battery for knowledge-graph competency evaluation
abstract: This record is a dated artifact record for a forthcoming paper, deposited before the paper exists and before the battery was run against the serving store. It argues from the published evidence that a language layer alone cannot certify its own answers. CodeSimpleQA measured the strongest frontier model at 62.9 percent on stable coding facts, with grounded retrieval near 71 percent against a parametric ceiling near 42 percent. GPTKB's 101-million-triple knowledge base built from a model showed only 31 percent of sampled triples verifiably true. KGQAGen's audit of 16 KGQA benchmarks found average factual correctness of 57 percent. The artifact is a 50-row human-authored refusal battery for knowledge-graph competency evaluation, frozen in advance: 40 knowledge rows, 8 refusal rows, 2 canary rows. The battery executes as a release gate against the live serving store, where an empty result over a complete schema is certified absence and a refusal is distinguishable from a failed retrieval. A paper describing the evaluation is under preparation. Files are restricted during the priority window as an independent-development record. Version 1, November 2026.

title: Integrating Trustworthy AI into CCAM: Enabling Uptake at Vehicle, Mobility Ecosystem and Industry Levels
abstract: This paper presents key insights from the AIthena project on trust-worthy and human-centric artificial intelligence (AI) to support large-scale deployment of Connected, Cooperative and Automated Mobility (CCAM) systems. It explores how AI can enhance perception, situational awareness and trans-parent decision-making to enable safe, explainable and context-sensitive automation. By addressing challenges across vehicle, mobility system and industrial level, the paper identifies technological and systemic enablers for a re-liable adoption. At the vehicle level, the project identifies critical weaknesses in current AI solutions, proposing enhancements through Explainable AI (XAI) to improve robustness and transparency across perception, scenario understanding and decision-making. It also addresses development challenges, including realistic data collection, complex testing and detailed reporting to meet transparency requirements. At mobility level, the project tackles AI trustworthiness in complex, mixed-traffic environments. It proposes methods to evaluate the reliability of V2X data and supports adaptive routing through AI-based reasoning models that integrate sensor data and behavioural context. At the industry level, the paper examines enablers such as standard alignment, regulatory frameworks and innovation ecosystem maturity. A preliminary roadmap is proposed for deploying explainable and accountable AI in CCAM, aiming to align technology, governance and user expectations to-wards sustainable, inclusive mobility in Europe.

title: QuaNor - a new language
abstract: Spin-state XNOR is the core resolution mechanism of Quanet's quanta model: each quanta carries a three-state spin (0, ½, or 1) plus a binary qubit, giving six possible states that pack base-6 into a byte stream. When two quanta sequences meet, a fabric compares them position by position — spin first, then qubit — and combines the two equality results with XNOR, yielding a resolved bit for each position. Those bits serve two purposes at once: they collapse overlapping quanta into a single observed state (1 keeps the left quanta, 0 the right), and they hash into a signature that chains each message to the previous one, making the sequence tamper-evident without URLs or a central authority. In short, spin breaks binary, XNOR resolves the overlap, and the result both selects the data and proves its order.

title: AI Literacy: An Exercise in Power-Knowledge
abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes one of the most significant systems of knowledge production in our society today, questions relating to who can access and shape that production grow increasingly important in our discourse. This paper argues that the existing frameworks for AI literacy, which are dominated by technical competency and responsible use principles, are insufficient be-cause they enforce a “consumer” orientation toward AI rather than fostering genuine epistemic agency. Based upon Foucault's concept of power-knowledge, Freire's pedagogy of critical consciousness, and scholarship of digital literacy, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of AI literacy as a critical practice that equips individuals not just to use AI systems, but to critically evaluate them, resist their structuring assumptions, and participate in their governance. The paper further argues that unequal access to AI tools in society recapitulates longstanding epistemic injustices, and that a literacy framework oriented toward empowerment must account for these structural inequities. A three-part framework of AI literacy based on the notions of contextual use, critical interrogation, and participatory governance, frame this literacy as a cultivation of epistemic “agents” rather than the training of competent consumer of AI-generated information. Preprint (author manuscript) of the paper published in the Proceedings of the Ninth AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2026), 9(3), 1745-1752. https://doi.org/10.1609/aies.v9i3.43263

title: Ferdinand of Bavaria (Elector of Cologne) to Maximilian I of Bavaria, Bonn, 22 December 1619 (BayHStA KAA 4591, DECODE R9426): ciphertext-only break of a numerical homophonic nomenclator
abstract: Ciphertext-only break of a numerical homophonic nomenclator cipher: letter from Ferdinand of Bavaria, Elector-Archbishop of Cologne, to his brother Duke Maximilian I of Bavaria, Bonn, 22 December 1619 (Bayerisches Hauptstaatsarchiv, Kurbayern Aeusseres Archiv 4591, ff. 281-286; DECODE record R9426). The key was rebuilt by annealing against a 16th-century German model and applied unchanged to the sibling letter R9425 as a control. 95.8% of 2,614 cipher tokens are read (count.py); the 74 open tokens are nomenclator groups. Contents: transcription, key, reading, English translation, scripts, validation data, control letter, notes and structured profile. Not included: the manuscript images, which are the archive's and are shown on DECODE (login required); permission to republish them has not been asked. The reading is fragmentary where clear-hand words and cipher words alternate; our notes record no review by a specialist. Prepared for the HistoCrypt 2027 Cipher Solutions track. See README.md in the archive.

title: Bitcoin and Ethereum: Computational Analysis of Twelve Years of Social Media Discourse, Sentiment Dynamics, and Sustainability Narratives
abstract: Description This data contains tweet IDs and derived variables for 42.7 million tweets tagged #bitcoin/#BTC (35,791,717 tweets, March 2010 – June 2022) and #ethereum/#ETH (6,873,450 tweets, November 2013 – June 2022), collected with snscrape in June 2022, before the Ethereum Merge. For every tweet the files give sentiment scores from four methods (VADER, Twitter RoBERTa, CryptoBERT, FinBERT), climate relevance from a keyword dictionary and from ClimateBERT, cleaning flags, simple text counts and engagement counts. For the climate-related subset they add the relevance and stance coded by a large language model (critique, defence, solution, info, promo) and the domains and source types of linked websites. A human-coded validation sample of 1,000 tweets, the keyword dictionary and the coding instructions are included. The files contain no tweet text, usernames or account information. Tweets can be retrieved by their IDs through the X API; the full data are available from the corresponding author for non-commercial academic research under a data use agreement. Files File Rows Contents BTC_derived_climate_sentiment_links.csv 35,791,717 One row per Bitcoin tweet: ID, date, tweet metadata, engagement counts and all derived variables (data dictionary below) ETH_derived_climate_sentiment_links.csv 6,873,450 The same for Ethereum tweets gold_key.csv 1,000 Validation sample: tweet ID, coin, sampling stratum, keyword and ClimateBERT result group_sizes.csv 10 Size of each sampling stratum in the full data, per coin (used to weight recall) gold_codes.csv 1,000 Human codes for the validation sample: relevance, stance, sentiment gold_codes_coder2.csv 250 Second coder's codes for the reliability check keyword_dictionary.md — Climate keyword dictionary: terms, tiers, exclusions codebook.pdf — Coding instructions for relevance, stance and sentiment README.md — This description The two derived files are joined to each other, or to the validation files, on id. A tweet tagged with both coins can appear in both corpora, so use id together with coin when combining them. How the data were collected and processed Collection. Tweets were collected with snscrape in June 2022 using the hashtags #bitcoin and #BTC (Bitcoin corpus) and #ethereum and #ETH (Ethereum corpus). The snscrape search returns original tweets, replies and quote tweets, so the corpora contain no retweets. Engagement counts (likes, retweets, replies, quotes) reflect their values at collection, not at posting. Sentiment. VADER compound scores (vaderSentiment package) were computed on the original tweet text. Twitter RoBERTa, CryptoBERT and FinBERT were run on every tweet, with user mentions replaced by “@user”, links by “http” and texts truncated to 128 tokens. Cleaning flags. Duplicate texts were identified after lower-casing and removing links, mentions, hashtags and extra spaces (the first copy is kept). Tweets with 8 or more hashtags, or more hashtags than half their words, are flagged as hashtag-stuffed. Climate filter. A three-tier keyword dictionary selected candidate climate tweets: 186,021 Bitcoin and 31,144 Ethereum tweets. ClimateBERT (climate detector) was run on every tweet as a comparison. Clean climate subset. Duplicates (checked among keyword matches) and hashtag-stuffed tweets were removed, leaving 130,574 Bitcoin and 15,500 Ethereum tweets. LLM coding. Each tweet in the clean subset was coded by a Claude model (named in llm_model) for climate relevance and stance, using the prompt in the paper's supplement. 92,386 Bitcoin and 10,647 Ethereum tweets were coded relevant. Links. For the relevant tweets, shortened links were expanded and each linked domain was assigned a source type. Validation. A stratified sample of 1,000 tweets (500 per coin) was coded by the first author, and 250 of them by a second coder. Agreement: relevance κ = 0.76, stance κ = 0.71, sentiment κ = 0.67. title: García de Toledo to Philip II, Messina, 16 July 1565 (AGS Estado leg. 1394 nos. 247 and 249): transcription, key and reading of two cipher letters from the Great Siege of Malta
abstract: Supporting material for a cipher solution submitted to HistoCrypt 2027: transcription, key, decoder, readings, English translations, working notes, statistical validation and the fixed-field profile for two duplicate cipher letters from Garcia de Toledo, viceroy of Sicily, to Philip II, written at Messina on 16 July 1565 during the Great Siege of Malta (Archivo General de Simancas, Estado leg. 1394 nos. 247 and 249; about 1,930 and 150 cipher groups, written in figures among clear Spanish). The cipher is a homophonic substitution on two-digit figures 12-43 in alphabetical order, with three figures for each vowel and one for each consonant; no word or name codes occur. The key was rebuilt from cribs in the clear Spanish beside the figures (adjacent plaintext). The key is simple and may have been recovered before: the claim is a reading of these letters, not a first break of the system. Both letters are read; open points are listed in NOTES.md (two word senses, one doubtful group, one single-occurrence sign). Our notes record no review of the readings by a specialist in sixteenth-century Spanish. Version 2 (21 November 2026) corrects decode.py, mk_validation.py and validation.tsv, whose run patterns decoded two clear dates as figures and skipped six b-initial runs; the key, the transcriptions and the readings are unchanged (see README.txt and the repository commit 8eb624c13f). Images are not included: they are the PARES (Spanish Ministry of Culture) images of the two records, https://pares.mcu.es/ParesBusquedas20/catalogo/show/3576569 (no. 247) and https://pares.mcu.es/ParesBusquedas20/catalogo/show/3576586 (no. 249). Write-up: https://cyphersolver.com/toledo1565.html. Source repository: https://github.com/dbourdeau/cyphersolver (folder targets/toledo1565).

title: MEO: Mining Reliable Expert Signals for Offline Reinforcement Learning in Wireless Networks
abstract: The operation of next-generation wireless networks increasingly hinges on Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) to optimize critical network decisions. Offline RL trains agents using accessible datasets and thus eliminates costly online interactions, rendering it particularly advantageous in dynamic wireless environments that demand low latency and high safety. However, its capability remains under-explored in wireless settings, where offline data are often limited and subject to partial observability. As a result, the learned policy fails to fully capture the informative decision patterns hidden in the dataset. To bridge this gap, we propose MEO, a framework that mines reliable expert signals from wireless datasets for offline RL deployment. MEO first identifies reliable expert samples from imperfect offline data, and then learns a structured latent representation to better distinguish expert and non-expert behaviors. Based on the representation, MEO further derives a compensable reward signal that helps offline RL algorithms more effectively exploit valuable expert knowledge. We evaluate MEO in three practical wireless network scenarios using datasets collected from real-world deployments. The results show that MEO consistently outperforms existing methods across all three scenarios. Notably, MEO can be seamlessly integrated with any offline RL algorithms, highlighting its generalizability and potential for wide adoption in wireless networks. (Code is available at https://github.com/lpzu/MEO)

title: Uncertainty-Aware Assessment of LLM-Enhanced Topic Models: An Experton-Based Approach to Interpretability
abstract: This study evaluates traditional, neural, and Large Language Model (LLM)-enhanced topic modeling approaches in a specialized tourism corpus. We compare Latent Semantic Indexing, Non-negative Matrix Factorization, Latent Dirichlet Allocation, Structural Topic Modeling, Neural LDA, and BERTopic, and then examine how LLM-based topic refinement affects topic representation, coherence, diversity, and interpretability. The results show that the LLM-enhanced BERTopic pipeline outperforms the traditional and neural approaches tested, achieving the strongest combined performance in topic coherence and topic diversity. The analysis also shows that decoding temperature influences both topic representation and LLM-based interpretability assessment, indicating that temperature should be treated as a substantive modeling parameter rather than a purely technical generation setting. Beyond model comparison, the study introduces an uncertainty-aware evaluation framework based on the Theory of Expertons, operationalized through M-expertons, to aggregate human and LLM judgments of topic interpretability while preserving uncertainty. Although the empirical application focuses on tourism, the proposed framework is relevant for specialized corpora in which topic interpretation involves semantic ambiguity, evaluator subjectivity, and uncertain boundaries between related themes.

title: A Recovered Average Is Not a Defended Corridor: What Adversarial Training Buys Spatiotemporal Traffic Forecasters, Why the Case That Static Methods Fail Rests on Node Selection While the Evidence of Failure Comes From Attack Shape, and the Evaluation That Would Tell Them Apart
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Spatiotemporal graph networks forecast speed and flow across road sensor networks, and a line of work since 2021 shows that a few perturbed sensors can wreck those forecasts. Whether adversarial training repairs the damage is disputed. One position, stated most sharply by the reinforced dynamic adversarial training (RDAT) paper at KDD 2023, holds that adversarial training designed for static domains does not carry over to traffic, because the attacker picks different victim sensors at each moment, and that defence needs a learned, time-varying choice of training nodes. A second position, from attack papers, time-series robustness studies and a 2025 study of forecasting foundation models, reports that ordinary adversarial training, or for the foundation models lightweight latent adversarial fine-tuning, already recovers most of the lost accuracy. A third, from a 2026 re-evaluation, holds that adversarial training tuned to norm-bounded perturbations barely transfers to targeted, congestion-shaped attacks, and that even training on the attack itself loses ground when the attack's reach changes. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the three positions are answering different questions under one word. A "dynamic attack" can vary in at least five things: which sensors it touches over time, the shape and size of the perturbation, the objective, the attacker's knowledge, and the metric used to score it. The dynamic-domain thesis concerns only the first. In RDAT's own main tables, adversarial training with randomly chosen nodes, the baseline RDAT presents as traditional adversarial training and elsewhere labels a dynamic strategy, closes about 93 percent of the attack-induced error on both benchmarks with Graph WaveNet, including against the time-dependent attack. Against that attack the learned selector adds less than two points of the gap, within run-to-run spread; under the other four attacks it stays within the spread on PeMS-D4 but adds 3.3 to 3.8 points on PeMS-BAY, slightly more than AT's seed spread. In the appendix, under the time-dependent attack, the ordering of the two methods flips with architecture while both close only 52 to 71 percent. Node selection is also the smaller lever in the attack literature's own ablations. The failures that are large come from changes in perturbation shape, target and metric. The paper consolidates the measured values in a table and a figure, states a procedure for crediting a robustness gain to a defence's dynamic component, and names the evaluations that would settle what remains open.

title: Just Talk Once: Communication-Efficient Split Federated LLM Fine-Tuning on Edge Devices
abstract: Large language model (LLM) fine-tuning is increasingly shifting toward data generated on edge devices, where memory, computation, bandwidth, and connectivity constraints make conventional federated learning difficult to sustain. Split federated fine-tuning (SFT) improves client-side efficiency by offloading most model parameters and computation to the server but requires step-by-step bidirectional communication loop across the split interface and forces continuous client involvement throughout training. In this paper, we present L-shaped SFT, a split fine-tuning framework that removes this bidirectional bottleneck. Our key insight is that weight tying in modern LLMs enables server-side hidden activations to be directly supervised using target embeddings, allowing the training loss to be computed on the server without returning server outputs to the client. To further eliminate the need for continuous client participation, based on L-shaped SFT, we introduce one-shot SFT, in which clients upload activations once and then go offline while the server continues optimization over cached representations. We implement our design in a real system testbed with heterogeneous edge clients, including commercial smartphones and NVIDIA developer boards. Experiments demonstrate that our schemes significantly reduce communication costs and client online time compared with existing SFT baselines.

title: Handling Data Heterogeneity in Edge IoT with Clustered Sequential Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning has emerged as an effective distributed solution to the limitations of centralized learning. It reduces the large volume of data that must be transferred to cloud servers when training machine learning models. Simultaneously, it improves privacy by allowing devices and users to keep their data locally. Instead of sharing raw data, only model updates, such as the gradients, are exchanged. However, it has limited performance at large scales, in contexts where data generated by thousands or millions of devices can be very heterogeneous and non-IID (non independent and identically distributed). In this paper, we propose a novel clustered sequential federated learning (CSFL) method, to address one of the main weaknesses of federated learning: data heterogeneity, which significantly impacts the convergence of the global model, as most existing methods fail to maintain good accuracy in highly heterogeneous environments. It's a hybrid approach that combines both sequential and parallel training in order to enhance accuracy, while accelerating the convergence speed of the global model. Based on clusters with balanced data distributions on each edge server, we train models sequentially using a knowledge distillation mechanism within each cluster to avoid catastrophic forgetting, aggregate them into an intermediate edge model, and finally combine all edge models in the cloud to produce a global model. We have evaluated CSFL through extensive experiments across various datasets (CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and TinyImageNet) and various configurations, notably levels of heterogeneity. The proposed method consistently demonstrates strong convergence behavior in highly heterogeneous environments without introducing any additional overhead.

title: Practical Perspectives on Machine Learning Interpretability for Public Transport Demand Forecasting
abstract: As data generated in public transport systems are growing in complexity and quantity, machine learning (ML) is increasingly used to model and forecast transport demand. While often highly accurate, the adoption of these techniques for optimizing operations and supporting decision-making is impeded by their low interpretability, which leads to a lack of trust from transport authorities and stakeholders. The aim of this paper is to explore the real-world applicability of ML-based prediction methods by evaluating current approaches from the contradicting perspectives of accuracy and transparency. In particular, we perform a fair comparison of the inherently interpretable NeuralProphet time series model, with the post-hoc interpretation of XGBoost using SHAP on real-world data from the metro line M4 of Budapest. Our results demonstrate that XGBoost outperforms NeuralProphet in terms of forecasting accuracy. Additionally, we show that the insights from the post-hoc SHAP analysis align both with the seasonality components of NeuralProphet and the characteristic morphologies of transport demand time series, supporting the adequacy of using SHAP to provide transparency for accurate black-box models. Source code is available at: github.com/galigergergo/PTDemComp .

title: Sharing of Irreversible Latent Features in lieu of RF IQ Data for Multiple Downstream Learning Tasks
abstract: Wireless in-phase and quadrature (I/Q) data is useful for training various radio frequency (RF) machine learning (ML) models. However, sharing such I/Q data faces barriers from concerns of (i) potentially violating laws related to recording raw samples that can eventually be decoded by an unauthorized third party, and (ii) revealing information about a proprietary system or the environment involved in the data capture. This paper proposes a different solution to sharing I/Q data intended for use in ML models by leveraging latent embeddings obtained through a shared encoder. The key contributions include: (i) demonstrating how a single set of common features can be extracted from an I/Q dataset for training multiple downstream RF classification or regression tasks, (ii) designing a method of structured noise infusion that impairs the reverse recovery of the raw I/Q from the feature space without significant impact to the downstream tasks, and (iii) demonstrating the application of this method on informative real-world, publicly available datasets. Sharing well-constructed yet privacy-preserving features can accelerate foundational research on ML for wireless without relying on hard-to-get I/Q samples.

The key contributions include: (i) demonstrating how a single set of common features can be extracted from an I/Q dataset for training multiple downstream RF classification or regression tasks, (ii) designing a method of structured noise infusion that impairs the reverse recovery of the raw I/Q from the feature space without significant impact to the downstream tasks, and (iii) demonstrating the application of this method on informative real-world, publicly available datasets. Sharing well-constructed yet privacy-preserving features can accelerate foundational research on ML for wireless without relying on hard-to-get I/Q samples.

title: The China AI Registry
abstract: A registry by Satoshi Yamauchi (Japanese title: 988の名簿) that transcribes every row of the attachments (delta lists) to the notices "Generative AI services filed (and registered)" published by the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC). Providing a generative AI service in China requires filing (备案) with the authorities, and the CAC publishes the filed and registered services with company names roughly every two months. Rows are transcribed from the attachment PDFs in their source column positions and characters; typos, column shifts and carry-overs are not corrected but recorded as observation codes, and each attachment is identified by the SHA-256 of its PDF. Only rows printed in an attachment PDF are admitted; no row is created from press reports, provincial cyberspace offices or company announcements, and every row of a connected attachment is admitted without exception. Each serial-number series is kept as its own table: filings, on-device filings, anthropomorphic-interaction filings, registrations and filing changes. Filing changes are appended without rewriting the original filing row. Only the author writes to the registry, with PGP-signed commits. The canonical data is data/registry.json; one CSV per table and data/sources.csv are generated from it. The data specification (docs/DATA_SPEC.md) and the update runbook (docs/UPDATE_RUNBOOK.md) are published with the data. The repository also contains a structural analysis of China's AI industry that uses the registry as its population, in Japanese and English editions. This archived version (v1.3.1, 22 November 2026) joins Attachments 1 to 14 (April 2024 to October 2026): as of 31 October 2026, 1,234 filings, 10 on-device filings and 1 anthropomorphic-interaction filing (1,245 in total, matching the CAC cumulative figure), 955 registrations and 1 filing change. Its text and data are identical to v1.3; v1.3.1 adds only the citation files. title: Does Switching to Muon Hurt Fine-Tuning of Small Open Models? A Case Study on Qwen2.5-0.5B
abstract: Muon, an optimizer that orthogonalises the momentum update of each weight matrix, has become a strong alternative to AdamW for pretraining language models. Whether it should also be used to fine-tune the many open models pretrained with AdamW is less clear, and recent studies disagree: one reports a penalty for switching optimizers on a narrow task, another finds none in broad instruction tuning. Both rely mainly on models pretrained from scratch or on models of 4B parameters and above. I examine the question for a small, heavily trained open model, Qwen2.5-0.5B, fine-tuned with AdamW and with Muon on a narrow task (WikiText-2) and on broad instruction data (a Tulu-3 subset), with a separate learning-rate sweep for each optimizer and three seeds for every final configuration. Switching costs little on the target task: validation perplexity rises from 12.47 to 12.53 in the narrow setting, and the target loss does not get worse in the broad one. Forgetting, measured as the increase in loss on held-out web text, is almost entirely determined by how far fine-tuning moves the weights (r ≥ 0.998 across 38 runs), and at equal target loss Muon forgets 1.7–2.3 times more in the narrow setting. Muon saved 6% of peak GPU memory and ran 9–10% slower. At this scale I find little reason to switch.

title: The Co-Development of Artificial Cognitive Capabilities: An Integrative Theoretical Framework of Interdependent Reconfiguration, Epistemic Warrant, and Future Reachability
abstract: The development of artificial intelligence is commonly characterized in terms of computational efficiency, model scaling, learning performance, generalization, and the successful execution of increasingly complex tasks. However, the emergence of autonomous agents, self-revising scientific systems, and open-ended learning architectures raises a more fundamental question: under what conditions does an intelligent system acquire genuinely new cognitive capabilities, rather than merely improve the efficiency of capabilities it already possesses?This article develops an integrative theoretical framework for understanding the co-development of artificial cognitive capabilities through functionally interdependent transformations. Its central proposition is that cognitive development depends not only on the performance of individual mechanisms of representation, action, observation, validation, and metacognitive regulation, but also on the organization of dependencies among these mechanisms.Drawing upon information theory, statistical comparison of experiments, active perception, causal representation learning, epistemic iteration, metareasoning, and open-ended learning, the framework distinguishes informational accessibility, operational capability, epistemically warranted capability, and the future reachability of cognitive capabilities.Several conditional results are developed through explicit formal constructions. First, complementary improvements may jointly enable a cognitive capability that remains inaccessible under either improvement separately. Second, locally advantageous decision rules may fail to discover productive developmental trajectories when benefits depend on coordinated transformations. Third, the order of cognitive transformations may affect developmental outcomes when operations involve prerequisites, noncommutativity, irreversible costs, or resource limitations. Fourth, agents possessing equivalent current capabilities may nevertheless differ in the range of capabilities reachable through subsequent development.The article further distinguishes functional improvement, epistemic progress, and developmental progress, demonstrating why improvements in internal evaluation scores cannot automatically be interpreted as genuine advances in cognitive capability.The proposed framework does not claim the discovery of a new law of information theory or a universal mechanism governing all forms of intelligence. Its contribution is integrative and explanatory: it provides a unified conceptual and formal structure for investigating how interdependent cognitive processes can jointly alter the accessibility, justification, and future development of artificial cognitive capabilities.

title: FedCRA: Client Risk-aware Aggregation via Update Reconstruction for IoT-based Federated Learning
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) enables distributed model training without sharing raw data, making it particularly suitable for Internet of Things (IoT) environments. However, FL remains vulnerable to poisoning attacks, where malicious clients manipulate local updates to corrupt global model optimization. Existing defenses mainly focus on updates within a single round and may confuse heterogeneous benign updates with malicious ones. In this paper, we propose FedCRA, a client risk-aware aggregation framework that exploits historical trajectories and trusted reference updates to reconstruct updates. Furthermore, the risk-aware aggregation jointly considers reconstruction gap, reference gap, and historical trajectory information to adaptively suppress suspicious updates. Extensive experiments under multiple poisoning attacks and heterogeneous data distributions demonstrate that FedCRA achieves stronger robustness than several representative aggregation methods while maintaining good scalability in large-scale FL.

title: LaSDAICVI: Children's Spanish Voice Commands Dataset
abstract: LaSDAICVI (LaSDAI Comandos de Voz Infantil) is a keyword-spotting dataset of Spanish speech recorded from 41 primary-school children aged 8 to 11 in Tucaní, Mérida state, Venezuela. It contains 29,061 isolated-word recordings (16 kHz, mono, 16-bit PCM WAV) of 60 keywords: the digits 0–9, the 32 results of the multiplication tables 2–9, and 18 voice commands. The release includes per-sample metadata (speaker ID, gender, age, grade), the official speaker-independent train/validation/test splits used in the thesis, background-noise clips for data augmentation, and the full B.Sc. thesis describing the recording protocol and baseline keyword-spotting models. Parents signed an informed consent form and each child signed an informed assent. The recordings are of minors: use them only for non-commercial research and education, do not attempt to identify participants, and do not use them for speaker identification, voice cloning or voice synthesis. Created at the Laboratorio de Sistemas Discretos, Automatización e Integración (LaSDAI), Universidad de los Andes, Mérida, Venezuela.

title: Strategic Client-Level Defense Placement in Mobile Federated Learning
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables mobile and edge devices to train jointly without centralizing private data, but compromised clients can poison the global model. When client-level protections cover only part of the population, a rational attacker can exploit predictable placement. We introduce SGDP-FL (Stackelberg Game-Based Defense Placement for Federated Learning), a budget-constrained Stackelberg game between a defender and an attacker. Before each round, the defender decides which clients to protect. The attacker observes this placement only through noisy reconnaissance, updates its belief about which clients are protected, and then chooses which clients to attack. We model the noisy observation as a Binary Symmetric Channel, and we model imperfect defenses by letting each protection block an attack only with a fixed probability. Monte Carlo estimation and a greedy knapsack oracle make the resulting bilevel problem tractable. We evaluate SGDP-FL on EMNIST, CIFAR-10, and CIFAR-100 under IID and non-IID partitions. The evaluation covers single- and multi-client attacks, with attack targets either fixed or periodically reshuffled. In every tested setting, SGDP-FL achieves the highest mean accuracy among Random, Highest-Value, and UCB allocation. Under multi-client attacks with periodic reshuffling, it raises CIFAR-10 IID accuracy from 55.68% for the strongest baseline to 59.78%, and CIFAR-100 IID from 32.42% to 34.49%. It also transfers to label-flipping and backdoor attacks and complements robust aggregation.

title: From Black-Box Computation to Causal Accessibility: Toward a Theory of Emergent Cognitive Capabilities in Artificial Intelligence
abstract: The increasing capabilities of artificial intelligence systems have intensified a fundamental question concerning the nature of machine intelligence: how can computational systems acquire cognitive capabilities that were neither explicitly programmed nor fully anticipated by their designers? Conventional explanations emphasize architectural complexity, parameter scaling, optimization, distributed representations, and the acquisition of increasingly sophisticated computational algorithms. Although these perspectives have substantially advanced the understanding of artificial intelligence, they do not completely resolve the distinction between information encoded within a system and information that can be functionally employed in generating intelligent behavior. This paper develops a theoretical framework centered on causal accessibility, defined as the context-dependent capacity of internally represented information to participate causally in task-relevant computational operations. The central hypothesis is that some changes in cognitive capability may arise not from the acquisition of fundamentally new representations or operations, but from changes in the functional accessibility, coordination, and compositional reuse of existing computational resources. The framework distinguishes representational availability, decodability, causal accessibility, compositional usability, and behavioral realization. It introduces a formal account of capability elicitation under fixed model parameters and specifies the conditions under which internal causal interventions could distinguish genuine functional access from mere informational correlation. Three theoretical propositions clarify why encoded information need not be behaviorally usable, why changes in accessibility can alter task performance without parameter modification, and why behavioral equivalence does not imply mechanistic equivalence. The proposed framework is situated in relation to mechanistic interpretability, causal abstraction, in-context learning, global workspace models, and theories of compositional intelligence. Its potential contribution is an integrated explanatory account of how latent computational resources may become operative cognitive capabilities. The paper does not claim to establish a novel fundamental law or provide new empirical findings. Instead, it offers a theoretically explicit and potentially falsifiable research program for investigating capability formation, emergence, and the organization of artificial intelligence.

title: PRISM: Reinforced Semantic Communication for Decentralized Federated Anomaly Detection in Vehicular Networks
abstract: Decentralized Federated Learning (DFL) enables collaborative learning that preserves privacy, but faces critical communication challenges in bandwidth-constrained environments such as vehicular networks. We propose Policy-driven Representation and Information Selection Method (PRISM), a Reinforcement Learning (RL)-based method that optimizes semantic communication in DFL through adaptive representation selection and intelligent topology management. Our dual-model architecture separates task learning (autoencoder-based anomaly detection) from communication control (Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO)-based decision making), enabling agents to dynamically select between transmitting full model weights or compressed trajectory embeddings. We formulate this as a Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) and train using a Centralized Training Decentralized Execution (CTDE) paradigm. We demonstrate our method through a digital twin monitoring scenario where vehicles collaboratively detect trajectory anomalies in neighbors' behavior in real time, and the logged detections support forensic analysis, insurance claims, and fleet auditing. Experiments on Simulation of Urban Mobility (SUMO) generated Barcelona traffic data show an F1-score of 0.90, scaling from 2 to 128 agents with graceful degradation past N = 32, Byzantine-robust aggregation, and validation on Next Generation Simulation (NGSIM) US-101 real traces (F1 0.82). The learned policy exhibits emergent temporal behavior: transmitting weights early during training when model divergence is high, then shifting to embeddings as models converge, with the weight-to-embedding mix derived as the equilibrium of the communication budget constraint. The method generalizes to other bandwidth-limited collaborative learning domains.

title: When to Trust a Knowledge-Graph Walk: An Empirical Study of Per-Hop Decision Confidence
abstract: LLM-based question answering over knowledge graphs is accurate but expensive, and it rarely says when an answer is likely wrong. We study an old design, in which each hop of a walk is a classification over the current node's relations plus STOP, with a zero-shot, swappable decider, and ask what the walk's path confidence is worth on MetaQA, WebQSP, CWQ and a 2WikiMultiHopQA evidence graph. Where walks fail often enough to matter (MetaQA 3-hop, WebQSP), path confidence ranks right above wrong answers well (AUROC 0.82-0.97): the most confident half of MetaQA 3-hop answers is 99% accurate (81% overall). With the model and prompt fixed, reading token probabilities beats stated confidence by 0.09-0.23 AUROC and matches or beats 5-sample voting at a fifth of its cost. Raw confidence is overconfident, but a two-parameter Platt fit repairs much of that. The walk is less accurate than an LLM writing the relation path in one call, cheaper only on Freebase, and its confidence fails on CWQ. title: S hear : Goal-Oriented Anomaly Detection on Compressed Time Series via Semantic Transition Graph
abstract: Sensor data in IoT systems are commonly compressed to meet resource constraints, yet anomaly detection directly on compressed data remains largely unexplored. This challenge is particularly evident for recurrent anomalies, which commonly appear as repeated abnormal patterns in long-running IoT streams. Existing approaches often become cumbersome or expensive since they decouple compression from analytics, requiring detection to reprocess full raw data, while supervised deep learning alternatives further demand labels or incur computational overhead unsuitable for edge deployment. In this paper, we propose Shear, a goal-oriented unsupervised method via Semantic Transition Graph (STG) induced directly from compressed time series. The STG organizes compressed representation as semantic states and encodes their temporal transitions, so that recurrent anomaly patterns are identified through unlikely state transition chains without decompression or neural network inference. Experiments on public datasets show that Shear achieves better detection performance than state-of-the-art approaches, while running 3.9× to 11.2× faster than subsequence-oriented methods and up to 2219× faster than deep learning baselines, with substantially reduced storage and memory footprint.

title: Joint Optimizing Federated Learning and Unlearning over Wireless Networks
abstract: In this paper, a communication and energy-efficient federated learning (FL) and unlearning (FU) co-designed framework is proposed. In the considered model, multiple edge devices collaboratively train a model. Users are allowed to quit the FL training and remove their data impacts on the trained model. Hence, an FU training is performed after the FL training. To reduce the energy and time consumption of FU, the users are grouped into multiple clusters such that the users in a group will retrain a deep learning model when the users in the group request to quit the FL training. The base station (BS) needs to determine the number of clusters, the users in each cluster, and the resource block (RB) allocated to each user, according to the probability that each user requests to quit the FL, data distribution, wireless channel conditions, and time and energy constraints. This problem is formulated as an optimization problem whose goal is to minimize the expected loss by determining the number of clusters, user cluster assignment, and RB allocations. This problem is challenging to solve since 1) the BS cannot predict which users will request data deletion in advance and 2) no explicit equation exists to capture the relationship between the number of clusters, user cluster assignment, and the expected FU loss. To solve the formulated problem, we first analyze the convergence rate of FU to build an explicit relationship among the FU training loss, the number of clusters, and the users in each cluster. Based on this relationship, the original problem is simplified to a mixed-integer optimization problem which can be divided into the user cluster assignment and the RB allocation optimization subproblems. These two problems are alternately solved by the designed Dinkelbach's method and the fast iterative shrinkage-thresholding algorithm (Dinkelbach-FISTA) and the standard Hungarian algorithm. Simulation results show that our method improves classification accuracy by up to 11.1% and achieves up to 3× faster convergence compared to gradient-based and ISTA-based methods.

title: Poster: ProbeGuard, Budgeted Active Probing for Safe LLM Service Recomposition under Silent Semantic Drift
abstract: Under silent semantic drift, an upgraded edge-cloud service stays schema-compatible but changes a unit, precondition, or state transition, invalidating LLM-orchestrated compositions. ProbeGuard treats candidate behaviors as a version space and spends a small budget of safe probes to discriminate them; owner-protected executable clauses cannot be weakened by an LLM, and a service is cleared only when all evidence-compatible hypotheses agree. In 252 controlled episodes, hybrid hypothesis generation recovers 94.8% of drifted behaviors, and ProbeGuard automates 98.4% of decisions correctly while cutting harmful clearance from 5.3% to 2.7% and latency from 0.94 to 0.56 s versus the strongest deployable baseline.
