title: PQ-FL-IDS: A Post Quantum Safe Federated Edge Intrusion Detection Scheme underlying 6G
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables Intrusion Detection System (IDS) models to be trained across Sixth Generation (6G) edge nodes without transferring sensitive traffic records to a central server. However, the model updates exchanged during FL-based IDS (FL-IDS) training remain exposed to interception and harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks by quantum-capable adversaries. This paper presents PQ-FL-IDS, a post-quantum (PQ) FL-IDS scheme for 6G edge networks. It protects model-update exchange using a real, non-simulated Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM-512, NIST FIPS 203), the Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode with a 256-bit key (AES-256-GCM), and per-round forward secrecy through ephemeral key pairs. Differentially Private Stochastic Gradient Descent (DP-SGD) with Rényi DP accounting further bounds record-level leakage from local updates. In each round, clients train locally with calibrated DP noise, encrypt the model update, and send only the protected payload for server-side aggregation. We evaluate PQ-FL-IDS on ToN-IoT with a 1D-CNN and FedAvg, and on CICIoT2023 with MobileNetV2-1D and FedProx, under baseline, PQC-only, and PQC+DP settings. ML-KEM-512 with AES-256-GCM adds less than 0.003% computational overhead relative to per-round training time and at most 3.5 KB of payload expansion, with no accuracy loss, and remains stable from 2 to 5 clients. The privacy analysis shows predictable ε growth with the subsampling rate and characterizes the privacy-utility frontier: formal budgets of ε = 0.9-2.4 are obtained for σ = 0.8-1.1, with a utility cost that depends strongly on task complexity.

title: Semantic Low-Code Data Fusion on the Edge to Support Intelligent Traffic Management
abstract: Intelligent traffic management applications require integrating data from diverse sources on the road infrastructure like radar sensors, cameras, and connected vehicles. The growing computational power deployed on the edge enables distributed computation of the data and near-real-time traffic control. However, interoperability is hindered by two key challenges: heterogeneous protocols for data access and inconsistent data semantics across sources. A data harmonisation solution is needed to retrieve data from different data sources while enabling a uniform representation of the information for data fusion and integrated analysis. The paper describes our solution to support the low-code definition of data integration pipelines by configuring a set of modular and reusable components. We leverage Semantic Web technologies and declarative mapping rules to resolve semantic inconsistency through a common conceptual model. A set of deployment templates enables the execution of the pipelines both on the cloud or on the edge to support diverse downstream applications with different performance and scalability requirements. Finally, the paper discusses the testing and validation of such a solution to support the reduction of collisions caused by unsafe braking at road intersections in a live deployment at the Mobility Lab in Helsinki.

title: Time to Protection in Federated Intrusion Detection on Jetson Orin Nano Clusters
abstract: Federated Learning (FL) allows IoT devices to improve a shared intrusion detector without exchanging raw data. A device, however, can only learn from attacks that reach it, and because federated detection is evaluated as a whole for the fleet of IoT devices or averaged over attack classes, it is not reported how long a device that has never observed an attack class remains exposed to it without protection. The aim of this paper is to measure that exposure window, round by round, and to determine how it depends on the share of the fleet that already holds the class. We deployed a federated system with nine clients on two Jetson Orin Nano clusters connected over a WAN. As the main dataset, we used N-BaIoT, which covers two devices that were never infected by the mirai attack. It was tested with one to seven attacked clients and validated on CWRU and PAMAP2 datasets. The results showed that new class arrival depends on the share of the fleet that already knows about it, reaching 0.827 on mirai after one round when trained from the start with mirai data on seven out of nine clients, and reaching protection thresholds after 4, 17, and 39 rounds for seven, three, and two of nine clients attacked, when the model was initially trained without knowledge of mirai. Our findings show that federation delivers recognition of an attack class quickly when much of the fleet already holds it, and slowly or not within our horizon when only a few devices have been hit, which is the case a defender is most concerned with.

title: Re-identification Risks and Privacy Challenges in Connected Vehicle Systems
abstract: CEDR’s Trusted Integrity and Authenticity for Road Applications (TIARA) project equips National Road Authorities with the tools and insights needed to develop secure and privacy-preserving data infrastructures for Cooperative Intelligent Transport Systems. In this paper we examine the privacy risks associated with C-ITS data, highlighting vulnerabilities in anonymisation methods and re-identification risks due to detailed data transmission, such as location and behavioural patterns. We explore state-of-the-art mitigation measures, including differential privacy, homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation, and federated learning. We also emphasize the importance of frameworks like pseudonymisation, data minimisation, and transparent data sharing. Our findings reveal significant privacy risks in C-ITS data, including vulnerabilities in anonymisation, re-identification threats through detailed data transmission, and the potential for behavioural profiling and location tracking. This emphasises the need for advanced mitigation measures, robust regulatory frameworks, and collaborative efforts among stakeholders to ensure secure and privacy-preserving use of connected vehicle data. Finally, we propose systemic and regulatory recommendation to road authorities, and provide a timeline from strategy to deployment based on short-, to mid- and long-term solutions.

title: Less Federation, More Personalization: One-Shot Multi-View Clustering for Federated Fall Detection
abstract: Federated learning is a natural fit for sensor-based fall detection, where data are privacy-sensitive and highly non-IID across subjects. A two-stage framework is proposed in which each client first learns label-free representations using FMMVCC, a multi-view clustering encoder that combines reconstruction, cross-view consistency, contrastive learning, and prototype-based objectives. The resulting encoders are then aggregated via a single round of FedAvg into a shared frozen feature extractor, decoupling representation learning from downstream classification. Experiments are conducted on the FallTL dataset, a wearable sensing benchmark evaluated under both binary (Fall/ADL) and 16-class (activity × Fall/ADL) granularities. Results show that FMMVCC achieves strong representation quality, outperforming four self-supervised baselines in binary classification (84.15% ACC) and providing competitive performance in the fine-grained setting. On top of these representations, the personalized closed-form classifier consistently outperforms FedAvg, FedProx, and shared analytic baselines by 8-13pp, and matches or exceeds FedProto in the 16-class setting while requiring no communication during inference. Finally, cross-client alignment metrics are shown to be weak predictors of downstream performance, while class-separability measures correlate more reliably with accuracy.

title: Continuous Passive Target Tracking over Intermittent and Narrow Sensing Beams in 6G Networks
abstract: 6G networks promise an advanced infrastructure for high-precision passive sensing and tracking, particularly in emerging sectors like Low-Altitude Economy (LAE) and Internet of Vehicles. However, realizing passive sensing in 6G remains challenging due to its unique signal characteristics, especially the extreme directionality of narrow beams and the intermittent availability of sensing resources, which are subordinated to the primary communication traffic. In this paper, we propose SPOT, a novel passive beam tracking framework that achieves continuous, high-precision tracking using only temporally sparse sensing slots. We employ an Interacting Multiple Model combined with an Extended Kalman Filter (IMM-EKF) to robustly predict non-linear target dynamics. We further develop a beam selection strategy that maximizes Fisher information gain to minimize tracking uncertainty, integrated with an opportunistic exploration mechanism to detect emerging targets. To reduce computation complexity, we introduce a lightweight approximation of the Posterior Cramér-Rao Lower Bound. Extensive evaluations using both simulations and real-world datasets demonstrate that SPOT significantly outperforms existing baselines, achieving a detection rate near 100% and an average tracking error below 1 meter, even in multi-target scenarios with highly sparse temporal updates.

title: FrozenSFL: Model-Frozen Split Federated Learning for Resource-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning over Heterogeneous Edge Devices
abstract: Collaborative fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) at the network edge enables privacy-preserving and personalized generative intelligence, but is constrained by the limited memory and compute resources of edge devices. Traditional approaches, such as split federated learning (SFL), partition models between devices and a server, requiring iterative exchanges of activations/gradients while the server manages multiple submodels. This leads to substantial communication overhead, high activation storage costs, and severe server-side memory pressure when scaling to massive heterogeneous devices. In this paper, we propose FrozenSFL, a resource-efficient SFL framework for collaborative fine-tuning of LLMs across heterogeneous edge devices. At its core, FrozenSFL strictly freezes device-side submodels to eliminate both deviceside backpropagation and server-to-device gradient transmission, thereby removing on-device activation storage requirements and downlink communication overhead. Building upon this design, we improve the framework in two aspects. First, we design a layerwise LoRA aggregation strategy to handle structural heterogeneity introduced by device-specific model partitioning and enable efficient server-side updates. Second, we introduce a server-side feature caching mechanism that reuses invariant features, allowing subsequent training epochs to proceed offline and reducing redundant computation and communication. We implement the FrozenSFL system as an asynchronous multi-threaded pipeline, which serves as our real-world testbed for evaluation. On the device side, forward computation and data transmission are decoupled via a producer-consumer mechanism. On the server side, a first-in-first-out scheduling strategy serializes fine-tuning tasks across devices. A hybrid memory-disk streaming mechanism further buffers incoming data and ensures stable training under network variability. Extensive evaluations with representative models, including BERT-Base (0.11B), ViT-Large (0.3B), and LLaMA-2-7B (7B), validate the effectiveness of FrozenSFL. evidence.title: FrozenSFL: Model-Frozen Split Federated Learning for Resource-Efficient LLM Fine-Tuning over Heterogeneous Edge Devices
evidence.abstract: Collaborative fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) at the network edge enables privacy-preserving and personalized generative intelligence, but is constrained by the limited memory and compute resources of edge devices. Traditional approaches, such as split federated learning (SFL), partition models between devices and a server, requiring iterative exchanges of activations/gradients while the server manages multiple submodels. This leads to substantial communication overhead, high activation storage costs, and severe server-side memory pressure when scaling to massive heterogeneous devices. In this paper, we propose FrozenSFL, a resource-efficient SFL framework for collaborative fine-tuning of LLMs across heterogeneous edge devices. At its core, FrozenSFL strictly freezes device-side submodels to eliminate both deviceside backpropagation and server-to-device gradient transmission, thereby removing on-device activation storage requirements and downlink communication overhead. Building upon this design, we improve the framework in two aspects. First, we design a layerwise LoRA aggregation strategy to handle structural heterogeneity introduced by device-specific model partitioning and enable efficient server-side updates. Second, we introduce a server-side feature caching mechanism that reuses invariant features, allowing subsequent training epochs to proceed offline and reducing redundant computation and communication. We implement the FrozenSFL system as an asynchronous multi-threaded pipeline, which serves as our real-world testbed for evaluation. On the device side, forward computation and data transmission are decoupled via a producer-consumer mechanism. On the server side, a first-in-first-out scheduling strategy serializes fine-tuning tasks across devices. A hybrid memory-disk streaming mechanism further buffers incoming data and ensures stable training under network variability. Extensive evaluations with representative models, including BERT-Base (0.11B), ViT-Large (0.3B), and LLaMA-2-7B (7B), validate the effectiveness of FrozenSFL. In particular, for LLaMA-2-7B, FrozenSFL can reduce device/server VRAM footprint by up to 14%/82.7% with only 1% accuracy loss, while achieving up to 6.7× fine-tuning speedup.

title: Open, Distributed Research Ecosystems for Intelligent Transport Innovation in Europe
abstract: Modern transport systems increasingly rely on complex, heterogeneous datasets to inform research, planning, and policy. However, centralized approaches to data storage and analysis face significant challenges: they compromise data sovereignty, increase transfer costs, and often limit reproducibility due to privacy and ownership constraints. Recent advances in federated models offer a paradigm shift, allowing algorithms to travel to the data rather than the reverse. This approach supports privacy-preserving processing while aligning with FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) principles of scientific data management. Within this architectural philosophy, the RAISE project has implemented a Mobility Pilot to explore the application of federated infrastructures in the transport domain. The pilot operates across three distributed computational nodes hosted by research institutions in Belgium, Spain, and Greece, applying federated analytic workflows to electric vehicle telemetry data. Analyses are executed locally on distributed nodes, validating a scalable, secure alternative to centralized analytics. Results demonstrate the feasibility of federated models in mobility research, offering insights into EV energy efficiency while ensuring reproducibility and data sovereignty. The study illustrates the potential of open, distributed research ecosystems to drive intelligent transport innovation across Europe.

title: Demo: Multimodal Stress Monitoring with Split Federated Fine-Tuning on Mobile Devices
abstract: We present an end-to-end mobile system for proactive stress monitoring from wearable signals. The framework is supported by an extensible split federated learning system that enables on-device LoRA fine-tuning of large language models. By analyzing physiological data, the application distinguishes emotional states, summarizes recent trends, and provides brief, actionable suggestions. Upon detecting a negative emotional state, the paired smartwatch or smartphone proactively delivers notifications to users to encourage mindfulness. The on-site demonstration will showcase real-time sensing-inference on smartwatch-phone pairs, alongside a recorded split federated learning process that continuously learns from user private data. Our code has been open-sourced at: https://github.com/HKU-WILL-Lab/Multimodal-Stress-Monitoring-with-Split-Federated-Fine-Tuning-on-Mobile-Devices.

title: Modal-Organizational Theory of Artificial Intelligence (MOTAI): Visual Atlas of Cognitive Organization, Capability Spaces, and Organizational Transformations
abstract: MOTAI Visual Atlas: Cognitive Organization, Capability Spaces, and Organizational Transformations This visual atlas provides a systematic graphical representation of the Modal-Organizational Theory of Artificial Intelligence (MOTAI), a conceptual and formal framework for investigating artificial intelligence through cognitive organization, functional capabilities, compositional structures, resource constraints, and organizational transformations. The atlas contains 17 pages of scientific diagrams, conceptual maps, comparative tables, and explanatory visualizations. It illustrates the central relationships between computational implementation, causal-functional organization, accessible cognitive operations, and the transformation of possibility spaces. Main components: The conceptual architecture and analytical levels of MOTAI. The formal organization of cognitive states, operators, admissible compositions, constraints, and resource costs. The distinction between actualized, operationally accessible, and transformationally accessible cognitive capabilities. Compositional closure and resource-bounded capability spaces. Four forms of cognitive and organizational transformation. Functional equivalence, capability comparison, and organizational incomparability. Seven formal properties and their conceptual implications. The relationship between structural organization, cognitive novelty, and changes in accessible capabilities. The visualizations are intended to support theoretical research in artificial intelligence, cognitive science, philosophy of computation, causal abstraction, and the study of complex intelligent systems. Scientific status: This atlas is a theoretical and conceptual resource. It does not present experimental findings or claim empirical validation. Its diagrams represent formal definitions, illustrative examples, and philosophical relationships rather than experimentally established neural mechanisms. Contents: A 17-page vector-based PDF visual atlas and a ZIP archive containing PNG versions of the atlas pages. Related research: The atlas accompanies the foundational MOTAI treatise and its independent formal model specification. Version: 1.0 (November 2026). Research framework: EMPIRAXIS Research.

title: mmPoison: Targeted Clean-label Poisoning Attacks on mmWave-based Human Activity Recognition
abstract: Nowadays, mmWave-based human activity recognition (HAR) systems are widely used in smart homes, healthcare monitoring, and telemedicine. To achieve high accuracy, HAR systems require large-scale data collection from distributed sources for model training, such as edge devices or public repositories, which opens up opportunities for attackers to inject poisoned data into the training process, inducing false predictions and damaging the reliability of mmWave-based HAR systems. This paper presents targeted clean-label poisoning attack strategies, mmPoison, which injects imperceptible poisoned data into the training datasets for causing misclassifications on target instances in mmWave-based HAR systems without controlling the labeling process. In mmPoison, different attack methodologies are proposed for different attacker capabilities. For white-box setting, discriminative region masking is used to limit perturbations in discriminative regions. Then, mmPoison updates perturbations based on parameter trajectory alignment, and optimizes the poisoned instances to remain close to the clean instances. This process is iteratively applied to generate poisoned datasets. For black-box setting, mmPoison trains surrogate models with pseudo-label supervision and then uses them in a generator-discriminator framework to generate poisoned instances by jointly optimizing attack effectiveness and imperceptibility. Experiments conducted on public and self-collected datasets validate the effectiveness and imperceptibility of mmPoison in causing misclassifications within mmWave-based HAR systems.

title: The AI Forecast Registry
abstract: An append-only registry by Satoshi Yamauchi (Japanese title: 予測の名簿) of public forecasts about AI. Each row records the statement verbatim in its original language, with the sentence before and after, the date and the primary URL; describes the form of the forecast (the presence or absence of a deadline, a subject, a magnitude and a resolution condition) independently of whether it proves true; and fills the outcome only with what the forecaster later said about their own forecast and what a primary source states as fact. No verdict by the recorder appears. Registration and outcome are recorded as separate PGP-signed commits, so that a third party can verify that a forecast was registered before its outcome was known. Only the author writes to the registry; every forecast that meets the admission criteria is admitted, whether it warns of danger, argues for safety or denies that a capability is near. The registry begins on 22 March 2023 with the Future of Life Institute's open letter "Pause Giant AI Experiments." Rows are never rewritten: outcomes are appended to the canonical data as separate records. The canonical data is data/registry.json; data/registry.csv (rows as registered) and data/outcomes.csv (appended outcomes) are generated from it. Japanese and English editions. This archived version (v1.1, 22 November 2026) holds 23 rows (5 recorded after resolution, 18 before) and is the first version archived after an outcome was appended to a row registered before resolution: row 009, whose deadline was the week of 21 to 27 September 2026. The registry is updated roughly once a month, and a new version is archived in each month in which an outcome is appended. AIをめぐる公開の予測を記録する、山内怜史による追記専用の台帳。各行は、発言を原文の言語のまま直前・直後の一文とともに逐語で記録し、発言日と一次URLを付す。予測の形(期限・対象・尺度・決着条件の有無)は、予測が当たるかどうかとは独立に記述する。帰結には、予測者本人が後から自分の予測について述べた言葉と、一次資料に記載された事実だけを置き、記録者の判定は書かない。登録と帰結は別々の署名付きコミットで記録し、予測が帰結より前に登録されたことを第三者が検証できる。台帳に書くのは著者一人であり、収載基準を満たす予測は、危険を警告するものも、安全を主張するものも、能力の到来を否定するものも、同じ基準で載せる。起点は2023年3月22日のFuture of Life Institute公開書簡「Pause Giant AI Experiments」。行は書き換えず、帰結は正本に別の記録として追記する。正本は data/registry.json で、data/registry.csv(登録時の行)と data/outcomes.csv(帰結の追記)はそこから生成する。日本語版・英語版を収録。この版(v1.1、2026年11月22日)は23行(決着後に登録5行・決着前に登録18行)で、決着前に登録した行に帰結を追記した後の最初の保存版である(009、期限は2026年9月21日から27日の週)。台帳は月に1回程度更新し、帰結を追記した月ごとに新しい版を保存する。

title: MODAL-ORGANIZATIONAL THEORY OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
abstract: One of the fundamental problems in contemporary artificial intelligence research concerns the relationship between the computational structures of intelligent systems and the cognitive capabilities they exhibit. Although artificial neural networks are typically described in terms of computational units, parameters, architectures, internal representations, and information-processing mechanisms, these descriptions do not fully resolve the conceptual distinction between operations currently performed by a system, operations that remain accessible under specified conditions, and transformations that may alter the system's repertoire of possible cognitive activities.This treatise develops a modal-organizational framework for analyzing artificial intelligence through the structure of its functional possibilities, the constraints governing their realization, and the transformations through which these possibilities may change.The central argument is that the organization of an intelligent artificial system cannot be adequately characterized solely by its currently realized computations. A broader analysis must also account for the relations between available operations, the conditions governing their composition, the resources required for their realization, and the permissible transformations of the organizational structures themselves.The proposed framework distinguishes five analytical levels: physical implementation, computational structure, causal-functional organization, compositional organization, and the modal structure of cognitive capabilities.A formal model of cognitive organization is introduced in terms of states, operators, composition rules, organizational constraints, and resource costs. On this basis, three categories of cognitive possibility are distinguished: actualized, operationally accessible, and transformationally accessible capabilities.The treatise further differentiates four types of organizational change: behavioral variation, compositional expansion, organizational-rule reconfiguration, and representational-space transformation.Four elementary formal propositions are developed concerning the invariance of capabilities under structure-preserving recoding, the insufficiency of restricted behavioral equivalence for establishing modal equivalence, the conservativity of adding an already definable operator, and the dependence of resource-bounded capabilities on implementation costs.The framework is examined in relation to causal abstraction, mechanistic explanation, functionalism, multiple realizability, computational mechanics, category-theoretic compositionality, dynamical systems, and theories of transformational creativity.A central conclusion is that novelty of output, novelty of capability, novelty of mechanism, and novelty of organizational principle must be treated as conceptually distinct phenomena.The proposed theory does not claim to establish a new physical constituent of intelligence or an empirically verified universal mechanism. Its contribution is a systematic philosophical and formal framework for examining the relationship between computational realization, organizational structure, functional possibility, and transformations of the space of accessible cognitive operations.

title: Human-Centric Trustworthy AI: AITHENA’s Methodological Framework for CCAM and Key Insights
abstract: This paper presents AITHENA’s human-centric, trustworthy AI methodology tailored for Cooperative, Connected and Automated Mobility (CCAM) systems. Recognising that public trust is essential to the adoption of AI-powered mobility, the framework translates high-level ethical principles, i.e., fairness, transparency, accountability, and privacy, into a practical Trustworthy AI qualitative checklist for developers, operators, and regulators. By integrating empirical user research on user mobility needs, expectations, and concerns, the methodology offers concrete tools to address trust challenges regarding AI in CCAM. The paper details how user perspectives are mapped to actionable checklist items, outlines implementation guidance, and discusses policy pathways aligned with the EU AI Act and automotive safety standards. Ultimately, AITHENA aims to bridge the gap between ethical theory and real-world application, fostering AI-driven mobility systems that reflect societal values and regulatory requirements.

title: Identity in the Age of AI: Toward a Functional Postphenomenology
abstract: Advanced AI systems increasingly mediate the cognitive and practical functions through which personal identity is enacted: intention formation, deliberation, memory, self-expression, preference formation, and relational interaction. Drawing on Western and Confucian conceptions of identity, this paper advances a functional hypothesis specifying six domains in which AI may be reorganizing the conditions of agency, and outlines the implications for responsibility, consent, dignity, and institutional design. The argument is functional and normative rather than metaphysical: not that agency disappears, but that the architecture of the self that is presupposed by our normative categories may require renewed examination.

title: Model choice and prompt framing in LLM sustainability judgments
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for sustainability assessment and decision support, yet their judgments may depend on the selected model and on how the task is defined. We compare 13 locally executed open-weight LLMs on 80 author-written sustainability scenarios using three prompt families that ask which actor should be responsible, bear the costs, or initiate action. Each model answered at two temperature settings with 100 repetitions, producing 624,000 deposited outputs, of which 610,708 contain a complete score vector. Scores were analyzed as relative actor support after removing each response’s overall level. Within this instrument, the cost prompt family produced the highest cross-model disagreement, exceeding both responsibility and catalyst by 7.37 points (question-cluster 95% intervals 5.56−9.15 and 5.38−9.36, describing variation across these 80 scenarios). It also produced the most lead-actor disagreement and the lowest full consensus. Moving from catalyst to cost reduced relative support for government and increased it for individuals and firms; moving from cost to responsibility largely reversed this pattern. These differences exceeded temperature-setting differences and persisted under model exclusion, alternative score transformations and tie rules, missing-response checks, and stems without explicit cost wording. Exploratory category patterns are conditional on uneven item coverage. Secondary rationale-language comparisons show the same within-model ordering but not the most cross-model variation under cost. Operational use should disclose model, prompt, and temperature choices; compare plausible alternatives; repeat generations; and refer high-disagreement judgments for human deliberation.

title: When Strong Reasoners Join the Pool: Small Union Premiums and Costly Runaway Generations in LLM Routing
abstract: Routing benchmarks often judge a router against a hindsight oracle that counts a query as solved whenever any model's recorded answer is correct, but under stochastic decoding that oracle mixes two different objects: the clairvoyant ceiling of committing to one model per query and the premium of calling several models and keeping any correct answer. A companion study measured this premium at 3.5 percentage points (pp) for 11 small open models on MATH-500; how large it is once current reasoning models enter the pool was unknown. We measure it with a fixed-protocol, pre-committed generation on a single NVIDIA B300: all 500 MATH-500 problems, 30 seeded samples per problem, Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and NVIDIA's Nemotron Nano 9B v2 and Nemotron Super 49B v1.5 (a NAS derivative of the same 70B) under vendor sampling, a 65,536-token cap, a pinned Math-Verify scorer, and an append-only attempt ledger, for 45,000 scored responses. The two reasoning models both reach 96.1% accuracy against 76.2% for the 70B baseline. The empirical product-coupling premium is 0.215-0.588 pp across all two- and three-model pools; the empirical plug-in selection headroom over always calling Nano is 1.27 pp; and resampling Nano three times gives practically the same empirical any-correct rate as calling all three models once. Only 31 responses reached the cap, 25 of them with exactly periodic tails, yet the capped responses account for up to 60.2% of a model's output-length-squared proxy, and long generations made a fourth planned model, Llama-3.1-8B, too slow to finish. The premium is far below the companion's 3.5 pp, but models, pool size and protocol changed together; an oracle gap should therefore be reported with the pool, the protocol, the samples per cell and the decoding budget that produced it.

title: Mytho-MoE: Knowledge Graph Datasets, Model Checkpoints, and Experimental Evidence
abstract: This record contains research artifacts for Mytho-MoE, a question-level mixture of domain-specific LoRA experts using a frozen Qwen3-4B backbone. The system includes independently trained Harivamsha (HVM) and Ramayana (RaMO) expert adapters, an original mixed-task router, and a router further adapted using graph-derived natural-language questions. The release provides author-constructed RDF knowledge graphs, instruction datasets, router-adaptation splits, evaluation questions and reference answers, saved predictions, aggregate results, model checkpoints, and a snapshot of the accompanying code. Dataset construction used English translations of the Harivamsha Purana and the Ramayana of Valmiki available through Wisdom Library, with AI assistance and manual review. Source URLs and construction details are documented in the accompanying files. The expert instruction datasets contain 200,248 accepted training records and 22,100 validation records. Evaluation cohorts overlap and should not be treated as independent samples. An audit identified 588 HVM validation rows with identical task, query, and target records in HVM training. The release documents this overlap and other evaluation limitations. Handwritten diagnostic questions were used during development. See the README and verification reports for file descriptions, checkpoint requirements, reproduction instructions, and limitations.

title: 可观察的定义(第二层):漂移、适应、维持(数字生命·草稿)
abstract: 可观察定义第二层。分段流、每段最优预测器、漂移 Δ_i(用上一段最优预测器预测新段多损失多少)、更新规则 U、适应代价;定义"维持":在阈值 τ、时长 T、代价预算 B_U 内,损失一直 ≤ τ;定义"可维持性"。本层"生命"最小定义 = 维持型系统:有持久状态、能按需更新、漂移下可维持、代价有界。观察性事实:漂移越大要的更新/代价越多;只优化当前段会遗忘旧段(回放缓解);跨段保留状态更省样本。可检验预测:漂移-代价曲线、更新频率-遗忘曲线、持久状态 vs 重置、固定预算下最优更新频率。对应原型:论文-56 的 noop/update 与旧内容重放就是本层定义的一个实例。

title: LFM2.5-24B-A2B
abstract: Preservation mirror. This Zenodo record is a long-term preservation mirror of the official Hugging Face repository LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B published by LiquidAI, mirrored byte-for-byte at the pinned revision 3dc4cd09c9a2a99e1e819693e79d3aba5e9bb4f2 (revision tree). The deposit contains the complete 27-file repository snapshot (47,964,603,149 bytes) exactly as published upstream — no file was modified, converted, quantized or re-sharded. An identical preservation copy is held at the Internet Archive: archive.org/details/liquidai-lfm2-5-24b-a2b-hf-preservation-2026-001. License: LFM Open License v1.0 — https://huggingface.co/LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B/blob/3dc4cd09c9a2a99e1e819693e79d3aba5e9bb4f2/LICENSE. The original license terms as published by LiquidAI govern; where the repository contains a LICENSE file it is included among the deposited files. The publisher's own model card (LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B @ 3dc4cd09) follows, reproduced in full. Try LFM • Docs • Discord LFM2.5-24B-A2B LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with only 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B. Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19. Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap. Efficient inference: Runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. Find more information about LFM2.5-24B-A2B in our blog post. 🗒️ Model Details Model Parameters Description LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base 24B (2B active) Pre-trained base model for fine-tuning LFM2.5-24B-A2B 24B (2B active) Post-trained for agentic workloads LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a general-purpose text-only reasoning model with the following features: Total parameters: 24.0B Active parameters: 2.45B Number of layers: 40 (30 double-gated short convolution blocks + 10 GQA) Experts: 64 per MoE block, top-4 routing Training budget: 36 trillion tokens Vocabulary size: 128,000 Context length: 131,072 tokens Languages: English, Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Spanish, Vietnamese, Thai, Indonesian, Hindi, Russian, Polish Generation parameters: temperature: 0.1 top_k: 50 repetition_penalty: 1.05 Model Description LFM2.5-24B-A2B Original model checkpoint in native format. Best for fine-tuning or inference with Transformers, vLLM, and SGLang. LFM2.5-24B-A2B-FP8 FP8 checkpoint (block-wise FP8 weights, dynamic FP8 activations). Best for high-throughput GPU serving with vLLM and SGLang with lower memory usage. LFM2.5-24B-A2B-GGUF Quantized format for llama.cpp and compatible tools. Optimized for CPU inference and local deployment with reduced memory usage. LFM2.5-24B-A2B-ONNX ONNX Runtime format for cross-platform deployment. Enables hardware-accelerated inference across diverse environments (cloud, edge, mobile). LFM2.5-24B-A2B-MLX-4bit MLX format for Apple Silicon. Optimized for fast inference on Mac devices using the MLX framework. LFM2.5-24B-A2B-DSpark DSpark draft model for speculative decoding with SGLang, for faster generation. Coming soon. We recommend using it for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. It is not recommended for knowledge-heavy tasks on its own: pair it with retrieval or web search, which plays to its tool-calling strength. Chat Template LFM2.5 uses a ChatML-like format. See the Chat Template documentation for details. Example: <|startoftext|><|im_start|>system You are a helpful assistant trained by Liquid AI.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user What is C. elegans?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant <think> You can use tokenizer.apply_chat_template() to format your messages automatically. [!TIP] 💡 Note: Unlike LFM2-24B-A2B, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a pure reasoning model that always thinks before it answers. It adds a <think> tag directly in the chat template when starting an assistant answer. Tool Use LFM2.5 supports function calling in four steps: Function definition: Provide the list of tools as a JSON object in the system prompt, or use tokenizer.apply_chat_template() with tools=.... Function call: By default, LFM2.5 writes Pythonic function calls (a Python list between <|tool_call_start|> and <|tool_call_end|> special tokens), as the assistant answer. You can override this behavior by asking the model to output JSON function calls in the system prompt. Function execution: Execute the call and return the result with the tool role. Final answer: LFM2.5 interprets the tool output and returns a plain-text answer addressing the original prompt. See the Tool Use documentation for the full guide. Example: <|startoftext|><|im_start|>system List of tools: [{"name": "get_candidate_status", "description": "Retrieves the current status of a candidate in the recruitment process", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"candidate_id": {"type": "string", "description": "Unique identifier for the candidate"}}, "required": ["candidate_id"]}}]<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user What is the current status of candidate ID 12345?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant <|tool_call_start|>[get_candidate_status(candidate_id="12345")]<|tool_call_end|>Checking the current status of candidate ID 12345.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>tool [{"candidate_id": "12345", "status": "Interview Scheduled", "position": "Clinical Research Associate", "date": "2023-11-20"}]<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant The candidate with ID 12345 is currently in the "Interview Scheduled" stage for the position of Clinical Research Associate, with an interview date set for 2023-11-20.<|im_end|> Training LFM2.5-24B-A2B keeps the LFM2-24B-A2B architecture with two changes: the context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and the vocabulary doubles from 65K to 128K tokens through an in-place tokenizer expansion for better non-Latin tokenization. Pre-training: ~33T tokens, up from ~17T. Mid-training: 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, then 300B tokens of long-context data at 131K context. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear in both phases. Post-training: supervised fine-tuning, teacher specialization, two multi-domain on-policy distillation stages (one non-agentic, one agentic), and agentic reinforcement learning inside popular agent harnesses (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, OpenCode), so the model learns their tools, system prompts, and interaction patterns. 🏃 Inference LFM2.5 is supported by many inference frameworks. See the Inference documentation for the full list. Name Description Docs Notebook Transformers Simple inference with direct access to model internals. Link vLLM High-throughput production deployments with GPU. Link SGLang High-throughput production deployments with GPU. Link — llama.cpp Cross-platform inference with CPU offloading. Link MLX Apple's machine learning framework optimized for Apple Silicon. Link — LM Studio Desktop application for running LLMs locally. Link — Quick start Get started with Transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0): from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextStreamer model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, device_map="auto", dtype="bfloat16", # attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" <- uncomment on compatible GPU ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) streamer = TextStreamer(tokenizer, skip_prompt=True, skip_special_tokens=True) prompt = "What is C. elegans?" input_ids = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], add_generation_prompt=True, return_tensors="pt", tokenize=True, )["input_ids"].to(model.device) output = model.generate( input_ids, do_sample=True, temperature=0.1, top_k=50, repetition_penalty=1.05, max_new_tokens=4096, streamer=streamer, ) Agentic Harnesses LFM2.5-24B-A2B supports tool calling for agentic workflows. Serve it locally with any OpenAI-compatible backend from the table above, then configure your agent harness to connect to it. For full setup instructions including installation and additional options, see our Agent Harnesses guide. Hermes Either use the interactive wizard or set it directly: hermes config set model.provider custom hermes config set model.base_url http://localhost:8080/v1 hermes config set model.default LFM2.5-24B-A2B hermes config set model.context_length 131072 hermes config set model.api_mode chat_completions hermes config set agent.tool_use_enforcement true OpenClaw Add to your config in `models.providers`: local: { baseUrl: "http://localhost:8080/v1", apiKey: "sk-local", api: "openai-completions", models: [{ id: "LFM2.5-24B-A2B", name: "LFM2.5-24B-A2B", contextWindow: 131072, maxTokens: 8192, cost: { input: 0, output: 0, cacheRead: 0, cacheWrite: 0 } }] } Pi Add to your config to `~/.pi/agent/models.json`: { "providers": { "local": { "baseUrl": "http://localhost:8080/v1", "api": "openai-completions", "apiKey": "local", "models": [{ "id": "LFM2.5-24B-A2B" }] } } } 🔧 Fine-Tuning We recommend fine-tuning LFM2.5 for your specific use case to achieve the best results. Name Description Docs Notebook CPT (Unsloth) Continued Pre-Training using Unsloth for text completion. Link CPT (Unsloth) Continued Pre-Training using Unsloth for translation. Example: <|startoftext|><|im_start|>system List of tools: [{"name": "get_candidate_status", "description": "Retrieves the current status of a candidate in the recruitment process", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"candidate_id": {"type": "string", "description": "Unique identifier for the candidate"}}, "required": ["candidate_id"]}}]<|im_end|> <|im_start|>user What is the current status of candidate ID 12345?<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant <|tool_call_start|>[get_candidate_status(candidate_id="12345")]<|tool_call_end|>Checking the current status of candidate ID 12345.<|im_end|> <|im_start|>tool [{"candidate_id": "12345", "status": "Interview Scheduled", "position": "Clinical Research Associate", "date": "2023-11-20"}]<|im_end|> <|im_start|>assistant The candidate with ID 12345 is currently in the "Interview Scheduled" stage for the position of Clinical Research Associate, with an interview date set for 2023-11-20.<|im_end|> Training LFM2.5-24B-A2B keeps the LFM2-24B-A2B architecture with two changes: the context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and the vocabulary doubles from 65K to 128K tokens through an in-place tokenizer expansion for better non-Latin tokenization. Pre-training: ~33T tokens, up from ~17T. Mid-training: 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, then 300B tokens of long-context data at 131K context. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear in both phases. Post-training: supervised fine-tuning, teacher specialization, two multi-domain on-policy distillation stages (one non-agentic, one agentic), and agentic reinforcement learning inside popular agent harnesses (OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi, OpenCode), so the model learns their tools, system prompts, and interaction patterns. 🏃 Inference LFM2.5 is supported by many inference frameworks. See the Inference documentation for the full list. Name Description Docs Notebook Transformers Simple inference with direct access to model internals. Link vLLM High-throughput production deployments with GPU. Link SGLang High-throughput production deployments with GPU. Link — llama.cpp Cross-platform inference with CPU offloading. Link MLX Apple's machine learning framework optimized for Apple Silicon. Link — LM Studio Desktop application for running LLMs locally. title: Federazione Semantica di Linked Open Data dell'Asia Orientale e Sud-Orientale, Ponti Cross-Dominio e Scoperta Automatica di Triadi Aperte Swanson ABC nell'Ipergrafo Rotta Aristeica Analisi Quantitativa di 11 Endpoint Live (#1240), 9 Vertici-Ponte Multi-Pilastro (#1242), Sensibilita' al Contesto Nullo Benjamini-Yekutieli e Demarcazione Fonologica (#1241- #1243)
abstract: La federazione di 11 infrastrutture Linked Open Data e Open Data dell'Asia Orientale e Sud-Orientale (5 nuovi endpoint W3C SPARQL 1.1 che portano la federazione da 24 a 29 nodi SPARQL attivi, affiancati da 6 distribuzioni RDF Turtle/JSON/XML API e dallo scarto documentato di 11 servizi non operativi) non genera di per sé alcuna scoperta automatica nel motore Swanson ABC fintanto che i nodi database e le sedi moderne restano isolati in quarantena (psca:swansonEligible=false) e i manufatti restano confinati a singoli articoli (78 triadi aperte complessive pre-ponti, 0 rigetti BY-FDR, score max 0.271811). Introducendo 9 vertici-ponte concettuali non geografici su 4 pilastri analitici (metallurgy_lia, linguistics_epigraphy, genetics_bio, material_cult_typology) e partizionando 4 iperarchi tematici di consenso (he728, he728_dongson_heger1, he728_kongorikishi_gandhara, he728_yayoi_bio_corridor) su 11.342 nodi @graph e 149.561 triple RDF SHACL-conformi, il numero di triadi aperte sale a 185 (Top-10 mediana +0.3295 vs baseline mono-dominio, MW p = 1.827e-04, Hedges g = 10.50). Dopo calibrazione su permutazioni, coda continua di Knijnenburg GPD e correzione conservativa Benjamini-Yekutieli (α = 0.05), emerge 1 associazione statisticamente significativa (Chang'an Q6501000 ↔ Linzi CHGIS hvd_85232, score = 0.73331, q_BY = 9.343e-05), mentre Cheonmachong (Gyeongju) ↔ Chang'an evidenzia un'istruttiva sensibilità al contesto nullo (q_BY = 0.01463 pre-#1243 vs 0.05921 post-#1243) e le piste Dian-Dong Son e Daisenryo Kofun rimangono ipotesi esplorative non significative a q_BY > 0.58. Parallelamente, gli audit #1241 e #1243 falsificano le convergenze grafiche tra Yaz (Tifinagh /z/), il carattere 木 (*C.mˤok > mù) su shuowen.space, 朱/銖 (*tjo/*djo > zhū [ʈʂu]) e i papiri di Cnosso. English Abstract The federation of 11 East and Southeast Asian Linked Open Data and Open Data infrastructures (5 new W3C SPARQL 1.1 endpoints expanding the federation from 24 to 29 active SPARQL nodes, alongside 6 RDF Turtle/JSON/XML API distributions and the documented exclusion of 11 non-operational services) yields no automatic discoveries in the Swanson ABC engine on its own, as long as database nodes and modern institutional locations remain quarantined (psca:swansonEligible=false) and artifacts remain confined to single publications (78 open triads pre-bridges, 0 BY-FDR rejections, max score 0.271811). By introducing 9 non-geographical conceptual bridge vertices across 4 analytical pillars (metallurgy_lia, linguistics_epigraphy, genetics_bio, material_cult_typology) and partitioning 4 thematic consensus hyperedges (he728, he728_dongson_heger1, he728_kongorikishi_gandhara, he728_yayoi_bio_corridor) across 11,342 @graph nodes and 149,561 SHACL-compliant RDF triples, open triads increase to 185 (Top-10 median +0.3295 vs single-domain baseline, MW p = 1.827e-04, Hedges g = 10.50). Following permutation calibration, continuous Knijnenburg GPD tail estimation, and conservative Benjamini-Yekutieli correction (α = 0.05), 1 statistically significant association emerges (Chang'an Q6501000 ↔ Linzi CHGIS hvd_85232, score = 0.73331, q_BY = 9.343e-05), whereas Cheonmachong (Gyeongju) ↔ Chang'an displays an instructive sensitivity to the null context (q_BY = 0.01463 pre-#1243 vs 0.05921 post-#1243), and the Dian-Dong Son and Daisenryo Kofun pathways remain non-significant exploratory hypotheses at q_BY > 0.58. Concurrently, audits #1241 and #1243 falsify graphic-phonetic convergences among Yaz (Tifinagh /z/), the Old Chinese character 木 (*C.mˤok > mù) on shuowen.space, 朱/銖 (*tjo/*djo > zhū [ʈʂu]), and the Knossos papyrus motifs.

title: MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake
abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/

title: Single-Transformer Latent Diffusion
abstract: Latent generative models typically rely on three separate networks: an encoder that tokenizes pixels, a generator that models the latent distribution, and a decoder that maps latents back to pixels. UNITE recently merged the first two into a single generative encoder trained in one stage, but its decoder remains a separate network. We ask whether this last network can be folded in too, so that one diffusion transformer encodes, generates, and decodes. Simply letting the shared backbone decode does not help. What makes it work is to cast all three modes as position-aligned sequence maps over one fully shared backbone, distinguished only by a mode token and the timestep. The resulting model, UNIFIED, is simple: one network trained from scratch in a single stage with only reconstruction and flow-matching losses, without adversarial losses or pretrained encoders (e.g., DINO). On ImageNet-1K 256x256 at matched parameters, UNIFIED improves gFID over UNITE at three sizes (~60M, ~115M, and ~215M) and reaches 2.08 with 215M parameters, the lowest among compared models under 250M parameters. On text-to-image generation, UNIFIED-B (218M) reaches a GenEval score of 0.87 at 512x512, exceeding single-stage pixel diffusion models with around one billion parameters. Full unification of latent diffusion is thus not merely feasible but beneficial.

title: NoHairCache: Calibrate-Once KV Cache Eviction with One Power-Law Exponent
abstract: The decay exponent α in KV-cache eviction is an intrinsic property of the model: calibrated once on a single corpus, it transfers directly across domains. Attention-based accumulation (H2O) and recency-based sliding windows (StreamingLLM) are two dominant eviction frameworks, often treated as unrelated, but we show that they are the two endpoints of a single power-law family: by scoring each token as s_i = A_i cdot (t-i)^{-α}, where A_i is cumulative attention and α controls the age penalty, H2O and StreamingLLM correspond to α=0 and αtoinfty, respectively (with StreamingLLM additionally hard-coding an attention-sink patch). The no-hair mechanism of xiang2026nohair bounds the admissible range of α, and the measured exponents agree: calibrating once on WikiText yields [0.556, 0.822] for a representative model (Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct). The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. NoHairCache achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM (p < 0.05 on all three datasets, with 0.06--0.10 PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget 512). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining 98.2% of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at 25% retention versus 91.1% for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.

The per-model ranges are consistent across five models (410M--1.5B) and independently match the optimal regions from perplexity sweeps. NoHairCache achieves the lowest perplexity across three datasets (WikiText, PG19, and arXiv) without per-dataset tuning, outperforming both H2O and StreamingLLM (p < 0.05 on all three datasets, with 0.06--0.10 PPL gains over StreamingLLM at budget 512). On downstream four-way multiple-choice QA, it matches or outperforms StreamingLLM across all nine (task, budget) cells, retaining 98.2% of full-cache accuracy on NarrativeQA at 25% retention versus 91.1% for StreamingLLM; per-cell McNemar tests are not significant, so QA is corroborating only. We release our calibration script and drop-in scorer upon publication.

title: Don't Sleep, Keep Watch: Proactive Perception for Computer-Use Agents
abstract: Computer-use agents (CUAs) built on vision-language models are increasingly entrusted with long-horizon tasks in live desktop, web, and mobile environments, where the screen keeps changing on its own. However, current CUAs lack real-time situational awareness: they perceive the environment through discrete snapshots, and the substantial inference latency of VLMs, compounded by highly dynamic interfaces, opens a perception-action gap in which the observed state frequently becomes stale before the corresponding action is executed. To bridge this gap, we present NightWatch, a plug-and-play framework that endows any CUA with continuous, temporally grounded perception without changing the agent's model, prompt, or action space. NightWatch couples the VLM agent with NightWatch-0.8B, a lightweight System-1 model that performs streaming monitoring of the interface state and keeps the agent synchronized with the evolving environment at low computational cost and latency, thereby grounding each decision in the current state rather than an outdated snapshot and reducing both stale actions and idle waiting while preserving task success. Experiments on desktop and dynamic web environments (OSWorld-Verified and DynaCU-Bench) show that NightWatch, driven by a watcher of only 0.8B parameters, reduces non-reasoning wall-clock time by 33% and wasted time by 53% on OSWorld while keeping task success on par, raises success on DynaCU-Bench from 39.5% to 44.2% with the large VLM agent, and is more efficient than passive-watching baselines such as AOI and PUSV under the same screenshot-only input, as well as a System-1 decision model more than 30times its size. Overall, NightWatch demonstrates that the timing of perception is as critical as its content, marking a step toward agents that maintain continuous awareness of their environment rather than perceiving it turn by turn.

title: NAT: Scaling Causal Neural Action Tokenizers Across Embodiments
abstract: Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.

title: Privacidad y seguridad en sistemas de aprendizaje federado: revisión de métodos y desafíos computacionales
abstract: Federated learning enables model training on distributed information without necessarily centralizing raw records. Nevertheless, parameter exchanges, participant coordination, and malicious behavior create threats that do not disappear when data remain at their source. This paper examines privacy and security safeguards in federated learning systems and their computational trade-offs. A structured narrative literature review was conducted through a targeted search of verifiable academic sources and thematic analysis of foundational studies, methodological contributions, and surveys. Findings distinguish inference and reconstruction attacks, model poisoning, backdoors, and server-related threats, and compare differential privacy, secure aggregation, robust optimization, and verification mechanisms. The reviewed literature suggests that no single method simultaneously guarantees confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Appropriate protection depends on the threat model, architecture, accuracy requirements, communication overhead, and computational constraints. Trustworthy deployment, therefore, requires complementary safeguards, explicit evaluation metrics, and reproducible tests tailored to each use case.

title: CivilCADBench: Benchmarking Multimodal LLMs for Understanding, Reconstructing, and Designing Civil Engineering Drawing Sets
abstract: Civil infrastructure is designed, built, and maintained through engineering drawing sets, yet preparing and revising them remains labour-intensive and calls for automation. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are promising candidates, but assessing them requires a benchmark grounded in real engineering practice. We introduce CivilCADBench, a benchmark for understanding, reconstructing, and designing civil engineering drawing sets, built from real infrastructure drawings and source CAD files containing over 250,000 CAD entities. Unlike parametric 3D CAD models, these drawings are dense, layered, and multi-sheet; and since prints are lossy projections with no pixel trace of layers, a file can print correctly yet remain wrongly organised. CivilCADBench comprises three task families of increasing difficulty: understanding tasks are evaluated with 2,183 expert-reviewed questions ranging from single sheets to whole sets, while reconstruction and design tasks are agentic, requiring models to rebuild printed pages as editable CAD files, either as single pages or entire drawing sets, and to produce new designs. These tasks are performed across 232 pages, 28 sets, and 19 design tasks, and evaluated by a deterministic scorer that compares model outputs with the designers' source files on geometry, layers, text, and dimensions. We evaluate seven frontier MLLMs on CivilCADBench, and find that they read and redraw printed content accurately but recover the file structure poorly: the best model scores above 90% in understanding and single-page reconstruction, yet only 60% on layer assignment and 48% on design. Grounded in real engineering practice, CivilCADBench exposes both the capabilities and the limitations of frontier models in professional civil engineering, laying a foundation for next-generation models and agentic systems for intelligent civil engineering.

title: Guarding with Judgment: Learning to Intervene for Multimodal Safety
abstract: When visual context makes an ordinary request unsafe to answer as asked, a blanket refusal may leave the user's need unresolved. Choosing how to help requires distinguishing an established hazard from a condition that still needs verification, a distinction that binary safety labels leave unspecified. We formulate this decision through four actions: allow, warn, review, and refuse. To ground these decisions in verifiable evidence, we build a corpus of 20,126 training audits and the JudiBench benchmark, connecting each action to diagnostic judgments, source evidence, and controlled context changes. Our guard, JudiAct, separately states what the source establishes, what condition governs the help, and how the rules apply. It then checks these three brief review items against the original inputs to predict diagnostic labels and a handling action. Supervised training learns individual judgments while comparing label assignments across related cases. A second stage swaps one review item at a time, using the resulting audit feedback to refine review generation. On JudiBench, JudiAct improves request and answer Macro-F1 by more than 28 percentage points over its 4B backbone. Across nine public benchmarks, it outperforms state-of-the-art guards on the mean delivered-answer score in both pre-generation and post-generation settings, cutting MM-SafetyBench attack success from 40.78% to 25.30%.

title: imr-anomaly-validation-ru: data and code for validating anomaly-detection algorithms on Russian regional infant mortality data, 2015–2023
abstract: Data and code for: Rusova V. S. Error Detection in Russian Infant Mortality Data: Validating Anomaly Detection Algorithms. Vestnik MIRBIS (version 2.0 of the article published as Vestnik MIRBIS, 2026, 1(45): 182–192, DOI 10.25634/MIRBIS.2026.1.20). The repository contains the regional panel of live births, infant deaths and the published infant mortality rate for 85 constituent entities of the Russian Federation, 2015–2023, reconciled cell by cell with the Rosstat operational bulletins included in data/raw; the computational scripts of all stages of the analytical protocol; machine-readable results of each stage, figures and execution logs; unit tests of the statistical methods; documentation of every analytical decision and a table linking each quantity reported in the article to the file in which it is computed. The analysis tests an anomaly-detection algorithm at three levels: its own computations, its operating characteristics on synthetic data with known anomalies and under admissible analytical specifications, and the limits of what is observable from aggregated data. A flag is a reason to check primary records, not evidence of an error; the absence of flags is not evidence that the data are free of distortion. Reproduce: pip install -r requirements.txt; python run_all.py (about one minute). Random numbers come from named streams derived from one seed (20260123), so runs are bit-for-bit repeatable. Licences: code under MIT (LICENSE); derived data, results and documentation under CC BY 4.0 (LICENSE-DATA). Files in data/raw are official Rosstat publications reproduced unchanged.

title: Self-WSP: Can Language Models Improve Themselves Through Weight-Space Programming?
abstract: Frontier language models can now read and edit the weights of a neural network much like code and thereby improve a small model, an approach known as Weight-Space Programming (WSP). We further explore applying WSP to a language model itself, which we call Self-WSP. Specifically, Qwen3.5-0.8B reads its own weights, proposes an edit, and then continues with the edited weights as both problem solver and editor. We find many cases of genuine self-improvement. Self-edits can raise GSM8K accuracy from 11.8% to 62.2% and MATH500 accuracy from 7.0% to 32.2%, sometimes by changing only 16 parameters, and in some cases repeated self-editing keeps improving the model. A closer look, however, reveals that these gains lack interpretability. The model shows little understanding of the edits it makes, and WSP driven by random search sometimes performs comparably. Self-WSP thus holds promise as a path toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), but realizing this promise requires further exploration.

title: Overcoming Challenges in AI Adoption
abstract: Brad Pitt's Billy Beane was rebuilding the Oakland A's with a radical, data-driven philosophy in a room full of people who thought he was nuts. He had the numbers. He had the model. And for the first 40 games, the model looked completely wrong. The team lost. The scouts laughed. The old guard declared victory.

title: Multimodal LLMs Know the Game but Assume the Real World
abstract: Multimodal large language models can state the rules of a video game, but do they apply them when they only see the game? We introduce RuleCraft, 1,240 image questions over 155 Minecraft rules with outcomes verified in the game engine, each asked in text, on the image with the game named, and on the bare image. Six widely used models know the rules and recognize the game, yet answer the bare image by real-world physics: naming the game raises their accuracy on rules where the game departs from reality by 8.2-19.8 points on a main set and by 33.8-52.7 on a hard stress-test set. Their errors pick the real-world outcome, the gap is largest where the game leaves a scene unchanged, and reasoning traces state the game's rule, then answer by reality. On the main set, naming the game mostly swaps the real-world default for the game's. The pattern holds with reasoning, recurs in two more games, and persists on questions the models themselves take to be about the game; one neutral sentence asking for the rules of the world shown recovers much of the gap. Evaluations that name the game measure knowledge of its rules, not world selection.

title: KMed-31B Technical Report
abstract: We present KMed-31B, a medical large language model post-trained from an open-weight model for on-premises deployment with limited hardware. Post-training a model for diverse medical tasks remains difficult, because improving one kind of task can lower performance on another. We attribute this to differences between tasks in expected output and available feedback. Medical question answering and diagnosis prediction have reference answers, whereas clinical inquiry has no single correct response and is judged with rubrics. We therefore divide medical training tasks into four categories by these two properties, train one specialist per category with a reward that its feedback supports, and integrate the specialists into a single student with Multi-teacher On-policy Delta Distillation (MOPD^2). For clinical inquiry, we build Synthetic Health Dialogue, a simulated corpus of consultations with lay users and clinicians whose patient cases span common clinical presentations in primary care. Relative to its base model, KMed-31B raises HealthBench Hard from 22.95 to 41.87 and HealthBench Professional from 37.92 to 50.20 in non-thinking mode, and from 23.80 to 51.48 and from 41.97 to 59.18 in thinking mode, while its scores on four multiple-choice medical benchmarks are maintained or slightly improved. KMed-31B has the highest unadjusted HealthBench Hard score among the compared models, including proprietary ones, and scores higher on HealthBench Professional than every open-weight model we compare, including models with more than ten times as many total parameters. Applied to another base model, Qwen3.8-27B, the same training recipe also raises both HealthBench scores. We describe the training recipe, data construction, and settings in detail so that institutions requiring on-premises deployment can develop medical models from open-weight foundations.

title: The Evaluation Substrate Matters: Benchmarking Multi-Agent Serving Substrates
abstract: Multi-agent systems (MAS) usually coordinate heterogeneous models and tools to solve complex tasks, creating a growing need for reliable evaluation. However, a multi-agent workflow that is fastest in one serving environment can lose its advantage in another, even when its models, prompts, and task remain fixed. This makes a benchmark result conditional on how the workflow is executed. We introduce MASSys, a benchmark for measuring this dependence in multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems. MASSys executes the same candidate-task pairs across serving substrates and load regimes, using five workload families spanning software repair, research synthesis, financial analysis, interactive control, and diagram generation. It records task quality alongside delivery, latency, cost, resource pressure, and failure evidence. In a controlled motivation diagnostic, the Star workflow falls from first to fourth in mean-latency rank under KV-cache pressure, while Chain rises from fourth to first. The substrate sweeps further show that increasing load creates long runtime tails and timeout pressure. In several task families, quality among evaluated outputs changes less than effective quality over submitted jobs: the system delivers fewer usable results even when the surviving outputs remain competitive. Tool and runtime traces reveal that these outcomes involve both model serving and non-model execution. Together, the results motivate evaluating MAS designs over explicit operating conditions and reporting which tasks are delivered, how well they are solved, and where execution breaks down.

The substrate sweeps further show that increasing load creates long runtime tails and timeout pressure. In several task families, quality among evaluated outputs changes less than effective quality over submitted jobs: the system delivers fewer usable results even when the surviving outputs remain competitive. Tool and runtime traces reveal that these outcomes involve both model serving and non-model execution. Together, the results motivate evaluating MAS designs over explicit operating conditions and reporting which tasks are delivered, how well they are solved, and where execution breaks down.

title: Physical regime changes expose formula misuse in large language models
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly employed for scientific computing across the Earth and environmental sciences, but problems in these fields often involve distinct physical regimes. LLMs may fail to recognize these regime-dependent constraints, applying formulas outside their domains of validity and producing plausible but physically incorrect results. We systematically investigate these failures through controlled experiments and assess whether post-training can improve regime-aware reasoning. Across 72 physical mechanisms, we find frontier LLMs frequently misapply formulas outside their regimes of validity, reducing accuracy by 13-57 percentage points. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards enables Qwen3.5-9B to match DeepSeek V4 Flash (284B) on regime-dependent tasks, but its effectiveness is limited by the formulas available in the base model. Combining supervised fine-tuning on a few worked examples with reinforcement learning improves accuracy by 61 percentage points, while distillation from a teacher supplied with the correct formula raises accuracy from 0% to 71%.

title: RecallWorld: Episodic Memory for Persistent Embodied Video World Models
abstract: Video world models generate plausible novel views but often lack persistent memory, failing to preserve a place's geometry and appearance when an agent revisits a scene. A central challenge is how previous views should be effectively used for creating memory. Reconstructing them independently underutilizes geometric constraints between nearby views, while repeatedly reconstructing a growing history can propagate later prediction errors into earlier geometry. We introduce RecallWorld, a persistent embodied video world model that jointly reconstructs short multi-view episodes into Scenelets while keeping geometry independent across episodes. Starting from a single source image, camera-aware ray lifting places perspective and native fisheye images in a common world frame, retaining wide-field content for perspective generation. Each generated segment extends the Scenelet memory and conditions subsequent generation. Coverage-based retrieval selects complementary Scenelets from the full history, while target-view visibility is resolved geometrically before appearance fusion, providing consistent memory conditioning for guiding subsequent generation. Across four datasets, RecallWorld improves revisit PSNR over the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.6 dB on partial revisits and 3.9 dB on full cycles, demonstrating substantially stronger preservation of scene identity across exploration and return.

title: Dual-Role Evaluation of Large Language Models in Cybersecurity: A Unified Framework for Offensive Generation and Defensive Intelligence
abstract: The rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) is reshaping cybersecurity by strengthening defensive capabilities while simultaneously enabling increasingly sophisticated offensive threats. Despite this dual-use nature, existing evaluation methodologies remain fragmented and commonly assess LLMs in isolation as either offensive or defensive systems. This work presents a unified dual-role evaluation framework that characterizes LLM behavior within a shared cybersecurity context through a multi-dimensional taxonomy encompassing role, capability, intent, and contextual use. The framework is empirically evaluated under a strictly single-turn setting (T = 1), in which each offensive input is independently assessed through one corresponding defensive response. The evaluation covers phishing detection, prompt injection, log analysis, malware reasoning, vulnerability exploitation, and incident response using malicious, benign, and ambiguous scenarios. Experimental results demonstrate strong overall detection performance, low error rates, and effective handling of dual-use and borderline cases through ambiguity-aware classification. The findings further reveal the difficulty of distinguishing malicious intent from structurally similar benign inputs, underscoring the importance of context-sensitive evaluation and uncertainty-aware decision making in cybersecurity applications. Overall, the study establishes a controlled and reproducible single-turn baseline for evaluating offensive inputs and defensive LLM responses across diverse cybersecurity tasks.

title: Seeing Right, Writing Wrong: Where Short Chain-of-Thought Breaks Spatial VQA
abstract: Asking a vision-language model (VLM) to think step by step often makes it worse at spatial questions, even though the image stays in context. We show that short chain-of-thought (CoT) turns a perception problem into a transcription problem. Once a VLM writes a spatial relation, its answer follows that sentence instead of the image, so whether CoT helps or hurts depends largely on whether the written relation is more accurate than answering directly. Studying 15 open VLMs (2B-38B) and six frontier closed models, we rule out token count, turn format, and visual forgetting in open models and trace the failure through three stages. First, writing re-weights visual cues, weakening a "lower is closer" shortcut in all 13 open models tested but also discarding valid cues, which produces false relations. Second, the written text takes over. With the model's own conclusion-removed rationale held fixed, swapping in an opposite-depth image moves the answer by 2-9 points on rendered twins (vs. up to 77 for direct answers) and by 3.0-3.4 points on average on natural photographs (vs. 20.5-69.6). Third, the concluding sentence can invert even a true relation, mainly on converse questions. Together, false relations and conclusion mis-mapping account for four in five CoT losses. Scale does not remove this bottleneck: Qwen3-VL-32B shows the same pattern. Frontier closed models are not hurt: they write relations as accurately as they answer, and three of six re-check the image after writing. The three queried with reasoning off lock in like open models, so re-grounding co-occurs with answer-turn reasoning; we identify answer-step re-grounding as the step open VLMs lack. In a single-model pilot, fine-tuning on fixed rationales with image-determined labels restores it on natural photographs. We open-sourced all our datasets and code at https://ming-zch.github.io/seeing-right-writing-wrong.

title: Métodos de inteligencia artificial explicable: revisión de técnicas, aplicaciones y limitaciones
abstract: La inteligencia artificial explicable (XAI) agrupa procedimientos orientados a facilitar el examen de predicciones, representaciones y comportamientos de sistemas de aprendizaje automático. Este artículo analiza las principales familias de técnicas, sus ámbitos de aplicación y sus limitaciones, mediante una revisión narrativa estructurada de publicaciones académicas verificables. Se incorporan elementos de búsqueda y organización documental empleados en estudios bibliométricos, pero no estima indicadores de producción científica ni declara exhaustividad. Se clasifican las propuestas en modelos intrínsecamente interpretables, explicadores locales aproximados, atribuciones basadas en contribuciones, métodos de gradientes, explicaciones contrafactuales y enfoques globales. Los resultados muestran que cada familia responde a una pregunta explicativa distinta y exige criterios particulares de evaluación. LIME aproxima decisiones individuales, SHAP distribuye atribuciones entre variables bajo supuestos definidos, los gradientes caracterizan sensibilidades en redes diferenciables y los contrafactuales identifican modificaciones capaces de alterar resultados. La utilidad de estos recursos se encuentra limitada por inestabilidad, dependencia de distribuciones de referencia, problemas de fidelidad, restricciones causales y divergencias entre evaluación técnica y comprensión humana. Se concluye que una explicación no debe equipararse con validación, causalidad, equidad o confiabilidad del modelo.
